#deck:Level Up! F2P
Who wrote the foreword to Level Up!, and what was his role?
column2: Danny Bilson, Executive VP of Core Games at THQ.

column1: Which two evergreen books does Bilson compare Level Up! to?
column2: A Scout Handbook and a Farmer's Almanac.

column1: Which game-design fundamental does Bilson single out?
column2: Doing one thing, well.

column1: Fill in: Very Important Thing #1 is 'Game designers have more ____.'
column2: fun

column1: What is Very Important Thing #2?
column2: No one on your team wants to read your design.

column1: How did Rogers get teammates to read his design docs?
column2: He drew them as cartoons.

column1: Why does Rogers say there's no single chapter about gameplay?
column2: Because every chapter is about gameplay. Even passive elements affect the player.

column1: Which two 'passive' elements does Rogers say still need gameplay thinking?
column2: Cutscenes and pause screens.

column1: What was Rogers' first job in the games industry?
column2: A 16-bit pixel artist ('pixel pusher' / 'sprite monkey').

column1: Name three games Rogers helped design.
column2: Any three of: Pac-Man World, Maximo, God of War, Drawn to Life, Darksiders.

column1: What genre do most of Rogers' examples come from?
column2: Single-player action games.

column1: Why does Rogers call 'I designed a game' an oversimplification?
column2: Games are made by many talented people. Claiming solo credit is wrong and egotistical.

column1: What career advice does Rogers give in a footnote about the industry's size?
column2: It's small, so don't make enemies. Be nice and hardworking and you'll go far.

column1: When is any approach to game design valid, according to Rogers?
column2: When it communicates the designer's ideas.

column1: What are the four audiences of the book?
column2: Working pros, future designers, students, and anyone who loves games.

column1: Why does Rogers prefer practical advice over theory for working pros?
column2: Mid-production you need nuts-and-bolts fixes. Theory suits conferences, not crunch-time problems.

column1: What's Rogers' formula for an aspiring designer with no mentor?
column2: Use the book as your mentor, be prepared, and seize the opportunity when it comes.

column1: Fill in: Rogers' acknowledgments lesson is that books don't ____ themselves.
column2: write

column1: What kicked off the writing of Level Up!?
column2: Cory Doctorow's glowing review of Rogers' GDC talk (then the publisher called).

column1: Your teammates skip your 12-page event spec. Which Press Start lesson applies, and what do you do?
column2: VIT #2 (nobody reads your design). Make a one-page visual spec: goal and KPI on top, mockups and a flow, numbers in a linked sheet.

column1: A teammate says the 'out of lives' popup is 'just UI, not design.' Which principle counters this?
column2: Every chapter (and screen) is about gameplay. That popup shapes whether players quit, wait, watch an ad or pay.

column1: Your new mobile game has 6 meta systems but a weak core action. Which foreword idea applies?
column2: Do one thing well: fix the core loop before adding meta.

column1: Why does Rogers say people who don't like playing games shouldn't make them?
column2: Making great games requires loving games. Those people should make room for someone who does.

column1: You want to break into F2P design. Which Acknowledgments lesson can you apply right now?
column2: Share work publicly. His GDC talk plus a review led to the book, so post teardowns and prototypes to create opportunities.

column1: Which two cheap first-page persuasion tricks does Rogers parody, and what does each stand for?
column2: A thrilling action excerpt (excitement hook) and a glowing quote from a famous person (borrowed authority). He drops both and promises honest, practical content.

column1: What does the footnote say about the fake "very famous game designer" quote?
column2: No such person exists, unless you count Shigeru Miyamoto, the creator of Mario. Rogers jokes he should have written it in Japanese.

column1: What were 16-bit pixel artists nicknamed, and why did Rogers leave that job?
column2: Pixel pushers and "sprite monkeys" (neither a compliment). He felt drawing with pixels was like drawing with bathroom tiles, and he heard the designers having more fun.

column1: Which pixel artists and teams does Rogers name as great 16-bit examples?
column2: Paul Robertson, plus the teams behind Metal Slug and the classic Capcom fighting games.

column1: Who are the two mentors Rogers names, and who requested the Platform Primer?
column2: Mentors William Anderson and David Siller. Jeremiah Slackza asked for the Platform Primer.

column1: Where do the Universal Truths and Clever Ideas appear in the book, and why?
column2: At the end of each Level, collected for the reader's convenience from lessons Rogers learned over his career.

column1: Your studio keeps burying A/B-test findings in a 30-slide deck nobody opens. Which Press Start idea fixes it, and how?
column2: Very Important Thing #2: no one wants to read your design. Make the findings visual and short (a one-page mockup with the goal and KPI at the top, numbers in a linked sheet).

column1: What three things make an activity a game, according to Rogers?
column2: At least one player, rules, and a victory condition.

column1: What is a video game, in Rogers' definition?
column2: A game played on a video screen.

column1: Why does hand ball break the 'players in conflict' definition?
column2: It needs only one player, so there's nobody to be in conflict with.

column1: What turns hand ball from a time-waster into a game?
column2: Adding rules and an objective (victory condition), which also creates a failure state.

column1: Which early video game was inspired by something as simple as hand ball?
column2: Tennis for Two.

column1: Whose definition of play is 'a voluntary effort to overcome unnecessary obstacles'?
column2: Bernard Suits (The Grasshopper, 1978).

column1: What is Danny Bilson's rule of thumb for a game's objective?
column2: Sum it up as simply as an old Milton Bradley board game did on its box.

column1: Which board game is the book's counterexample of a too-complex objective?
column2: Mouse Trap.

column1: Fill in: Battleship's box objective is to sink all of your ____'s ships.
column2: opponent

column1: Name the three lab-era games Rogers lists, with years.
column2: OXO (1952), Spacewar! (1962), Colossal Cave (1976).

column1: Where did the first video game programmers work?
column2: University computer labs (like MIT) and military facilities like Brookhaven National Laboratory.

column1: What was the first arcade video game, and when?
column2: Computer Space, 1971.

column1: Who created Computer Space, and what inspired them?
column2: Future Atari founders Ted Dabney and Nolan Bushnell, after playing Spacewar! at the University of Utah.

column1: Where were the first arcade games found, before dedicated arcades?
column2: In bars.

column1: What are vector graphics?
column2: Images constructed from lines (e.g. Asteroids, Battlezone, Star Castle).

column1: What are raster graphics?
column2: Images built from a grid of dots called pixels (e.g. Galaxian, Pac-Man).

column1: Why did color raster graphics matter for game characters?
column2: They made cartoon-style characters possible, and Pac-Man and Donkey Kong became pop icons.

column1: Name the three early-1980s arcade cabinet styles.
column2: Uprights, cocktail tables, cockpits.

column1: What was Virtual World's BattleTech Center?
column2: A steampunk arcade with linked battle pods where 8 players fought in virtual mechs.

column1: Why did the arcade golden age end?
column2: Elaborate cabinets needed floor space and costly maintenance, and late-1990s home systems matched and then beat arcade graphics.

column1: What replaced video games in many arcades?
column2: Redemption machines (like claw games) and skill games like Skee-Ball.

column1: What's the difference between a LAN center and an internet café?
column2: Both rent play time. LAN centers mix retail and social space for PC and console play; internet cafés emphasize a café atmosphere.

column1: What is a 'dark ride'?
column2: An amusement-park ride past scenes of (usually) animatronic characters, like Pirates of the Caribbean.

column1: Which game-ified dark ride also came home on the Wii?
column2: Toy Story Midway Mania (2008).

column1: What two features set home consoles apart from arcade machines?
column2: Multi-purpose controllers (many buttons, triggers, analog sticks) and swappable media (cartridge, CD, DVD).

column1: Which game and handheld made handheld gaming take off?
column2: Tetris on the Nintendo Game Boy (1989).

column1: What were the first handheld games limited to?
column2: One game per device (e.g. Auto Race, Game & Watch).

column1: Why did the keyboard lead to new PC genres?
column2: It allowed much richer input than arcade controls, which created text adventures.

column1: Which input device does Rogers credit for the rise of the FPS?
column2: The mouse.

column1: Which genres does Rogers say remain strong on PC?
column2: Strategy, FPS and MMOs.

column1: What does a game genre describe?
column2: The style of gameplay.

column1: What sets fighting games apart from other action games?
column2: The depth of their player controls.

column1: What is action-arcade's emphasis?
column2: Twitch gameplay, scoring, and short play time.

column1: What separates the shooter subgenres from each other?
column2: The camera view (first person, behind the player, or arcade-style views).

column1: What is the trade-off of the FPS camera vs third person?
column2: Tighter and more limiting, but more personal.

column1: What is the player's avatar usually in a shmup?
column2: A vehicle (like a spaceship) rather than a character.

column1: Three things MMORPGs are known for?
column2: PvP, repetitive grinding, and group battles called raids.

column1: What defines survival/horror?
column2: Surviving a horror scenario with limited resources, like scarce ammo.

column1: Fill in: the four X's of RTS are expansion, exploration, exploitation and ____.
column2: extermination

column1: Why does turn-based strategy allow more strategy than real-time?
column2: The slower pace gives players time to think.

column1: Name two hybrid games the book uses to show genre mixing.
column2: Grand Theft Auto (five genres) and Tuper Tario Tros. (Super Mario Bros. + Tetris).

column1: Who made the original Prince of Persia single-handedly?
column2: Jordan Mechner (he even composed the music).

column1: Why is placeholder art called 'programmer art'?
column2: Early programmers made all the art, and it was blocky and crude.

column1: What does a technical artist do?
column2: Supports all artists, e.g. rigging models for animators and teaching new tools.

column1: What is the designer's core role, regardless of title?
column2: Create the ideas and rules that make up a game.

column1: What do system designers define, per the book?
column2: How game elements relate to one another, e.g. the economy or tech tree.

column1: What do level designers do, per the book?
column2: Make paper maps, build grey-box worlds, and populate levels with enemies and treasure.

column1: Why do producers often become the 'face of the game'?
column2: They're the one team member who can keep all the moving parts straight.

column1: What three skills does a good tester need?
column2: Patience, persistence and great communication.

column1: How does game music differ from film music, per Rogers?
column2: Game themes are usually very short or must repeat over and over.

column1: What two kinds of sound cues does a sound designer create to help the player?
column2: Positive sounds (doing well, good loot) and warning sounds (danger, bad choices).

column1: List the five reasons game writers get hired.
column2: Rewrite the story, write dialogue, clarify prompts, write the manual and fiction support, add star power.

column1: What six things do publishers do?
column2: Fund, manage production, handle legal, manufacture, PR/marketing, distribute.

column1: What is the creative manager's 'thousand-foot view'?
column2: An unbiased, high-level outside view of a game that roots out design and construction weaknesses.

column1: What does a publisher's technical director do in due diligence?
column2: Assesses whether a new team can actually make the game it's being hired for.

column1: Your event spec says 'collect stuff to win stuff'. A teammate can't explain the goal. Which Level 1 idea applies?
column2: Bilson's box test: state the objective in one clear sentence (Battleship, not Mouse Trap).

column1: You're designing an idle game with no final ending. How do you keep it game-like per Rogers' definition?
column2: Add clear short-term victory conditions (stage clears, chapter goals, event milestones), since games need a victory condition.

column1: Your pitch: 'Tower defense meets card collection meets live PvP.' Which Universal Truth backs it?
column2: Genres come in all shapes and sizes: mix and match.

column1: Apple's ATT disrupted your UA overnight. Which Universal Truth applies?
column2: Technology never stops advancing, so keep adapting or get left behind.

column1: A designer says 'level 88 sucks' in review. What does Rogers demand instead?
column2: Explain WHY with specifics (cause, evidence, fix). 'It sucks' is never acceptable.

column1: Players keep missing a critical cue that's only a sound. Mobile fix?
column2: Back every audio cue with a visual (and haptic) one, since many mobile players play muted.

column1: In a modern F2P studio, who owns currencies, sources and sinks?
column2: The economy designer.

column1: In a modern F2P studio, who owns the event calendar?
column2: The LiveOps designer.

column1: How does a modern F2P product manager differ from the book's?
column2: The book's PM is a publisher-side schedule, milestone and payments manager. The F2P PM owns KPIs, roadmap and A/B testing.

column1: What two numbers must a UA manager keep in the right relationship?
column2: LTV must exceed CPI (lifetime value above cost per install).

column1: Your rewards for a new event would double players' weekly booster income. Who should flag it?
column2: The economy designer (sources vs sinks, inflation risk).

column1: Fill in: Level 1's last Universal Truth says making video games takes many different kinds of ____.
column2: people

column1: Fill in: arcade designers' 'continue?' countdown is the ancestor of F2P's '+5 ____' offer.
column2: moves

column1: Why does Rogers say you need a simple objective?
column2: If you can't sum up the objective quickly and clearly, players (and your team) won't get it, which signals a design problem.

column1: Why did consoles let players play many kinds of games when arcade cabinets couldn't?
column2: Their controllers had enough buttons, triggers and analog controls for variety, and swappable media replaced one-game boards.

column1: Why did longer PC sessions matter for genres?
column2: Time at the computer allowed longer experiences, so simulations, construction/management and strategy games grew.

column1: Why were laserdisc games like Dragon's Lair rare exceptions?
column2: They needed laserdiscs to play animated video footage, unlike normal sprite-based hardware.

column1: Why does Rogers say even placeholder sound effects matter?
column2: Games come alive once sound is added, and sound carries gameplay information.

column1: Why does Rogers advise would-be 'idea people' to choose design over writing?
column2: Game writers are usually hired late as freelancers, while designers create the ideas and rules.

column1: Why is specialization increasing on game teams?
column2: Games keep getting bigger, more complex and longer to make.

column1: Why do composers need a distinct style to get hired?
column2: Designers hire the sample matching the style in their head, and unique music that fits stands out (Danny Elfman effect).

column1: Why does the claw-machine footnote matter to F2P designers?
column2: Games that feel rigged destroy trust. Fair, transparent odds (like winnable Japanese claws) keep players.

column1: You're pitching a match-3 with a renovation story to a publisher. Which genre lesson are you using?
column2: Mix and match genres (puzzle + construction/management + story), like GTA or Tuper Tario Tros.

column1: Your runner's hazards are hard to read at speed. Which book genre's lessons should you study?
column2: Platformers, the runner's ancestor (jumping through challenging environments with readable hazards).

column1: A teammate wants a feature with 4 new currencies in the first session. Which Level 1 warning applies?
column2: The Mouse Trap problem: too many systems blur the objective. Introduce them gradually.

column1: You're in QA at a mobile studio and want to become a designer. What does Level 1 say?
column2: Testing is a classic gateway: testers become designers, artists, producers and studio heads. Learn fast and prepare.

column1: Your event shipped with a misconfigured reward that gave away premium currency. Which modern role should have caught it?
column2: QA (live event config checks), with the economy designer reviewing reward values.

column1: Your CPI is rising and installs are falling. Which role and team do you call?
column2: The UA manager with the creative/ad team (new video and playable ads).

column1: You need to know whether last weekend's event lifted D7 retention. Who do you ask?
column2: The data analyst (cohort and A/B analysis).

column1: A studio asks you to judge an outside team's prototype without bias. Which book role are you playing?
column2: Creative manager, giving the thousand-foot view.

column1: Fill in: A creative manager's best benefit is the 'thousand-____ view'.
column2: foot

column1: Fill in: Placeholder art is nicknamed '____ art'.
column2: programmer

column1: Fill in: Miyamoto created memorable characters with an 8-bit CPU and ____-bit pixels.
Which two scholars' definitions of "game" does Rogers say try too hard to sound smart, and what does each claim?
column2: Chris Crawford (1982): a closed formal system that subjectively represents part of reality. Kevin Langdon (1979): a contest of players in conflict with each other.

column1: What does "n00b" mean, and where did the word spread?
column2: Short for "newbie", someone new to a game. It predates the Internet but spread through online communities, and it implies inexperience.

column1: What defines a platformer, and what was its status at one time?
column2: A mascot character jumps (or swings, bounces) through challenging platform environments, sometimes with shooting or fighting. It was once the most popular subgenre (Mario titles).

column1: What is the emphasis of stealth games, and what are two examples?
column2: Avoiding enemies instead of fighting them directly: the Metal Gear series and Thief: The Dark Project.

column1: What is a beat 'em up (hack 'n' slash)?
column2: You battle wave after wave of enemies that grow harder (Double Dragon, Castle Crashers).

column1: What is the RPG subgenre based on, and how do players progress?
column2: Pen-and-paper RPGs like Dungeons & Dragons. You choose a character class and grow stats through combat, exploration and finding treasure (Knights of the Old Republic, Mass Effect).

column1: What do players do in a graphical adventure?
column2: Use a mouse or cursor to click around, uncover clues and navigate (Myst, Monkey Island, Sam & Max).

column1: What separates life simulation from construction/management?
column2: Construction/management: build and expand a place with limited resources (SimCity, Zoo Tycoon). Life sim: build and nurture relationships with artificial life forms (The Sims, Princess Maker).

column1: What are pet simulators descended from, and what do they revolve around?
column2: Tamagotchi digital pets. You nurture animals through feeding and relationships (World of Zoo).

column1: How wide is the music/rhythm genre, and what format do party games usually use?
column2: Music/rhythm: match a beat to score, from Simon to Rock Band. Party: designed for several competing players, usually as minigames (Mario Party, Buzz!).

column1: How does the book define puzzle games?
column2: Games of logic and pattern completion, either slow and methodical or reliant on hand-eye coordination (The Incredible Machine, Tetris).

column1: What is the sports management subgenre?
column2: You manage players or teams rather than playing the sport (FIFA Manager, NFL Head Coach). Sports franchises often ship annual versions.

column1: What is tower defense, according to the book, and how new was it in 2010?
column2: A relatively new subgenre on PC and handhelds where you build automated projectile-firing towers that hold enemies back (Defense Grid, Lock's Quest).

column1: What is vehicle simulation's goal, and what are its two subgenres?
column2: Make piloting or driving feel as "real" as possible. Subgenres: driving (race and upgrade vehicles) and flying (for pleasure, combat or space).

column1: Which other classifications does the book say cut across several genres?
column2: Adult games, serious games, advert games (advergames) and vehicular combat.

column1: In what order did game teams evolve, per Rogers?
column2: Solo creators (Prince of Persia), then two or three programmers, artists joining as players wanted better looks, design by whoever had the idea, and finally a dedicated design role. Specialization keeps growing.

column1: What specializations does the book list for programmers?
column2: Tools programmers, physics/simulation programmers (realistic water, inverse kinematics) and sound-tools programmers. Some freelance as contract "hired guns".

column1: Which art roles does the book list?
column2: Concept artist, storyboard artist, 3-D modeler/environment artist, texture artist, VFX artist, UI artist, animator, technical artist and art director.

column1: How did 3-D reach games in the book's history?
column2: Film first (Tron, 1982; Luxo Jr., 1986), then pre-rendered 3-D in Myst (1993) and Donkey Kong Country (1994). True 3-D existed in Battlezone (1980), and the 1994 PlayStation pushed realistic 3-D at home.

column1: Which hand-drawn, hand-animated games show what better hardware allowed artists?
column2: Darkstalkers (Capcom, 1994) and Metal Slug (SNK, 1996).

column1: How many fields are on Jesse Schell's "well-rounded designer" list that Rogers endorses?
column2: 19 fields, from the arts (animation, visual arts, music, sound design) and people skills (psychology, anthropology, public speaking) to economics, mathematics and technical writing.

column1: List the producer's responsibilities.
column2: Hire and build teams, write contracts, contribute to design, manage the schedule, balance the budget, resolve disputes between creative and programming leads, represent the team to management and publishers, coordinate outside art/music/cutscenes, and arrange testing and localization.

column1: When do producers usually join and leave a project?
column2: They are typically the first team member on and the last off.

column1: What is "quality assurance", and how long does it take?
column2: QA is just the test department. Reaching the publisher's quality bar takes weeks, if not months, of thorough testing.

column1: What are the publisher-side product manager's duties?
column2: Manage the team against the agreed schedule, help set production priorities, act as go-between with the publisher's legal department, review and approve milestones, pay the studio, and work with the ESRB for a rating.

column1: What is the ESRB?
column2: The Entertainment Software Rating Board, which determines a game's rating in the US.

column1: What is a "build" (or "burn")?
column2: An in-progress version of the game that can be played on a computer or special console.

column1: What has Rogers done as a THQ creative manager?
column2: Helped teams create and develop games, written pitches, worked with licensors on concepts, played builds to keep them true to the core idea and fun, and supplied press materials with marketing and PR.

column1: What does a publisher's art director do?
column2: Like a creative manager for art only: helps shape a visual style, suggests new directions, globalizes the visual language so it is clear to the player, and works with marketing on packaging and promotional assets.

column1: What does business development do at a publisher?
column2: Builds relationships with studios, runs pitch meetings, reviews demos, makes deals with outside studios and scouts emerging studios to acquire.

column1: Match the publishing role: negotiates contracts and watches for legal trouble; builds marketing strategy and print material; handles press events; runs the test department.
column2: Lawyer; brand manager; PR manager; QA manager.

column1: Who are talent recruiters, game reviewers and licensors?
column2: Recruiters place people with developers and publishers. Reviewers play games before release and write reviews and interviews. Licensors work for entertainment companies and make sure their brands are represented properly in games.

column1: Why is the Vectrex the footnote exception to the console definition?
column2: Its processor, screen, controller and a game were all in one self-contained portable unit (Smith Engineering, 1982).

column1: How far did handheld power travel in the book's story?
column2: From the digital blips of Mattel Football to the Sony PSP, whose processor can run the equivalent of a PlayStation One game.

column1: Name the three elaborate arcade cabinets Rogers highlights.
column2: Tail Gunner (Vectorbeam, 1979, back-to-back cockpit), Star Trek (Sega, 1982, Captain Kirk's command chair) and Out Run (Sega, 1986, a moving Ferrari Testarossa).

column1: How did late-1990s arcade games change?
column2: They turned into mini theme-park rides: rideable race horses, gyroscopic simulators and fighting booths where you used real punches and kicks.

column1: What did Rogers recall about the BattleTech pods?
column2: Photo-booth-sized cockpits with dual joysticks, foot pedals and banks of working dipswitches. Learning every switch took about a half-hour session.

column1: What does the footnote say about the Nintendo DS and Game & Watch?
column2: The DS has several design similarities to the original Game & Watch devices, which Rogers says is no surprise.

column1: Why were mobile games growing in 2010, according to Rogers?
column2: Phone games are quick and less expensive to make, so the number of mobile developers exploded in a few years.

column1: Which designer task does Rogers postpone to later in the book?
column2: Making sure the game is "fun".

column1: Fill in: Bilson says a game's objective should read as simply as an old ____ board game box.
column2: Milton Bradley

column1: State Level 1's five Universal Truths in your own words.
column2: 1) A game needs a player, rules and a victory condition. 2) Keep the objective as simple as a classic board game box. 3) Genres come in every shape, so mix and match. 4) Technology keeps advancing, so adapt. 5) Making games takes many kinds of people.

column1: Which filmmaker does Rogers quote on good ideas bordering on stupid ones?
column2: Michel Gondry

column1: Which game is 'a prince rolls junk into balls to rebuild the stars'?
column2: Katamari Damacy

column1: Why should you never dismiss a game idea for sounding stupid?
column2: Many hugely successful games sound absurd when described plainly, so silliness says nothing about potential.

column1: What are Rogers' five ways to get inspired?
column2: Read something unusual; walk/drive/shower; attend a lecture; play a (bad) game; follow your passion.

column1: Why do games start to feel derivative, according to Rogers?
column2: Developers love and draw from the same sources (games, comics, movies), so themes and mechanics get recycled.

column1: Will Wright named which three unusual sources of inspiration?
column2: Japanese gardening, architecture and biology

column1: Why does a walk or shower help generate ideas?
column2: A familiar routine occupies the conscious brain, freeing the subconscious to wander and make new connections.

column1: Why play a BAD game for inspiration?
column2: You see what was done poorly and practice figuring out how to fix it, which teaches more than admiring a good game.

column1: Pokémon grew out of Satoshi Tajiri's love of ____.
column2: collecting insects

column1: David Jaffe turned his love of whose movies into God of War?
column2: Ray Harryhausen's

column1: What is a 'designer's idea' in marketing speak?
column2: A concept the designer would love to play but marketing thinks the general public won't buy.

column1: Which game was the predecessor of The Sims?
column2: SimCity

column1: Which game was the predecessor of PaRappa the Rapper?
column2: Simon

column1: Which game does Rogers name as Braid's predecessor?
column2: Blinx: The Time Sweeper

column1: Whose shoot-'em-up evolution chart inspired Rogers' platformer chart?
column2: Raph Koster's (A Theory of Fun for Game Design, 2004)

column1: What did Donkey Kong add to the platformer?
column2: Jumping, plus a power-up that could defeat enemies

column1: What did Mega Man add to the platformer?
column2: Themed stages ending in themed bosses whose powers you gain after defeating them

column1: What was unusual about falling in Dark Castle?
column2: Falling didn't kill you immediately; you ended up in the dungeon. The hero could also hide.

column1: Crash Bandicoot used 3-D models and environments to create which named camera view?
In the platformer timeline, Ghosts 'n Goblins added ____.
column2: multiple weapons incl. projectiles, health as armor that breaks off, and boss monsters

column1: What do gamers want, in Rogers' all-caps answer?
column2: GOOD GAMES

column1: Why do designers need passion and vision, according to Rogers?
column2: Most gamers don't know what they want until it's shown to them, and players can sense passion.

column1: Name Rogers' seven wish-fulfillment feelings.
column2: Powerful, smart, sneaky, successful, rich, bad, heroic

column1: Who said all good game characters are wish fulfillment?
column2: Tim Schafer

column1: Why decide casual vs hardcore early?
column2: Setting the audience early lets you rule out design decisions right away.

column1: A 10-year-old usually wants a game made for what age?
column2: About 13 (kids want games for slightly older kids)

column1: What are the three kid limitations Rogers lists?
column2: Small hands can't do complex controls; ages 6–7 and younger may not read complex words or long text; watch the swearing.

column1: List Marc LeBlanc's 8 kinds of fun.
column2: Sensation, Fellowship, Fantasy, Discovery, Narrative, Expression, Challenge, Submission

column1: Why does Rogers find the 8 kinds of fun of limited use in the field?
column2: Ideas that sound fun on paper may not be fun when built, or may be fun only to you; fun is subjective.

column1: Why do developers lose objectivity about fun?
column2: They replay the same content hundreds of times, and fun fades with repetition.

column1: State the Theory of Un-Fun.
column2: Start with a fun idea; remove everything un-fun as you develop; what remains should be the fun.

column1: What's the caveat of the Theory of Un-Fun?
column2: The starting idea must be fun, or after removing the un-fun you're left with nothing.

column1: Name Rogers' typical un-fun culprits.
column2: Crappy camera, lousy controls, bad animations, too hard, too easy

column1: A producer's advice to Rogers: 'Don't be too ____.'
column2: dear

column1: What five things do you need to brainstorm?
column2: A working brain, something to write with, something to write on, a place to work, collaborators

column1: Why should brainstorm invitees understand how games are made?
column2: Otherwise you waste time on unrealistic ideas.

column1: What are the slots on Rogers' back-of-box template?
column2: Catchy slogan, 3 exciting images, 3 gameplay features, legal info, dev and publisher logos, rating, platform, barcode

column1: Why imagine a black-and-white 16-page manual for your idea?
column2: The constraint forces you to strip the idea to its bare essentials.

column1: Which writer's block trick comes with a warning, and what is it?
column2: Jump ahead to the good stuff: last resort only, since skipping drudge work can wreck schedules, budgets and the team.

column1: What is Miyamoto's 'wife-o-meter'?
column2: He shows ideas to his wife; any she hates get thrown away.

column1: Your team says the FTUE is fine, but you've all played it 300 times. Which principle applies?
column2: Loss of objectivity: get fresh outside players (wife-o-meter) and apply the Theory of Un-Fun.

column1: Your F2P concept's FTUE drop-off spikes at a long tutorial popup. Which principle?
column2: Theory of Un-Fun: find the un-fun and remove or fix it.

column1: Marketing calls your quirky mobile concept unmarketable. What's the Rogers-plus-F2P move?
column2: Don't fold or ignore them: test it cheaply (ad creative test, prototype) and let data decide.

column1: You're designing a game for 8-year-olds. How should the art and tone feel?
column2: Slightly older (aimed at around 10-year-olds), never babyish; keep controls simple and text minimal.

column1: You keep making clones of the top chart. Which inspiration habit fixes this?
column2: Read something you normally wouldn't: get inputs from outside games.

column1: You're stuck on the shop UI and want to design the boss event instead. What should you do?
column2: Use the other tricks first (narrow focus, walk, clear distractions, change room); jump ahead only as a last resort and don't miss deadlines.

column1: What's the F2P equivalent of the back-of-box exercise?
column2: A store page (title, icon, first 3 screenshots, captions) plus a short video ad with a 3-second hook.

column1: Kids reject games aimed at their own age as 'a game for my little ____'.
column2: brother

column1: Rogers' back-of-box exercise also asks how you would explain the game in a black-and-white ____-page manual.
Rogers' joke name for getting ideas while sitting outside in the sun: vitamin ____.
column2: Duh

column1: Your idea board has 40 features and they all seem good. Which truth applies?
column2: Don't be too dear: cut even good ideas that don't fit or that exceed what you need.

column1: A teammate says your survivor-like is just a copy of an existing hit. How do you answer in Rogers' terms?
column2: Most design builds on predecessors; the question is what new idea you add (steal and transform, don't photocopy).

column1: Your casual puzzle has a 10-minute minimum session. Which audience lesson is broken?
column2: Casual players don't want long grinds; pick the audience early and design for bite-sized sessions.

column1: Who is the hero of Dark Castle, and what two firsts does the game bring to the platformer timeline?
column2: Duncan. He can hide from enemies, and falling no longer means instant death: you land in the dungeon.

column1: Which companies are credited in the platformer timeline for Space Panic, Pitfall!, Pac-Land, Ghosts n Goblins and Dark Castle?
column2: Space Panic: Universal. Pitfall!: Activision. Pac-Land: Namco. Ghosts n Goblins: Capcom. Dark Castle: Silicon Beach Software. (Donkey Kong, Popeye, Mario Bros., Super Mario Bros. and Mario 64 are Nintendo.) Ideas jump across companies.

column1: What is Rogers' resolution of the story vs gameplay debate?
column2: A game doesn't need a story, yet it always has one (every play creates a narrative).

column1: What is step 1 of the classic story structure?
column2: A hero who has a desire

column1: In the classic structure, what happens right after the hero's first attempt?
column2: The method fails.

column1: Classic structure step 5 is a ____ of fortune that causes more trouble.
column2: reversal

column1: What are steps 6 and 7 of the classic structure?
column2: An even greater problem with greater risk; then one last problem with the most risk of all.

column1: What does every story ALWAYS have?
column2: A beginning, a middle and an end

column1: Which two standard structures does Rogers say you needn't be chained to?
column2: Joseph Campbell's Hero's Journey and Syd Field's Three Act Structure

column1: Name two other media Rogers suggests borrowing story structure from.
column2: Any two of: songs, TV news reports, Homeric poems, non-Western storytelling

column1: If gameplay is the meat, story is the ____.
column2: salt

column1: What does 'narrative' literally mean?
column2: An order of events

column1: Why do story-less games like Tetris still produce narratives?
column2: Humans perceive time linearly, so they experience and retell play as an ordered sequence of events.

column1: What is the designer's job regarding player narratives?
column2: Anticipate as many possible narratives as practical and make them all fun, building rising emotional states.

column1: What three variables does Left 4 Dead's Director use to estimate stress (per the book)?
column2: Health, skill and location (among others)

column1: What does Left 4 Dead's Director adjust?
column2: Number of attacking zombies, items generated (ammo, health) and the music

column1: Name Rogers' three examples showing almost anything can be gameplay.
column2: Mr. Mosquito, SimCity, PaRappa the Rapper

column1: In Rogers' Little Red Riding Hood game, what does the full picnic basket act as?
column2: A gating mechanism (it unlocks Grandma's house, the next level)

column1: What game element does 'what big eyes you have' become?
column2: A quiz, a puzzle or a rhythm game

column1: What are the three corners of the production triangle?
column2: Time, Quality, Money (choose two)

column1: What are the three corners of the Triangle of Weirdness?
column2: Characters, Activities, World

column1: How many Triangle of Weirdness corners may you make weird?
column2: Only one

column1: Why make only one corner weird?
column2: More weirdness alienates the audience; people feel they 'didn't get it', and nobody likes to feel stupid.

column1: Which corner is weird in The Wizard of Oz?
column2: Characters

column1: Which corner is weird in Star Wars?
column2: World

column1: Which corner is weird in Monty Python and the Holy Grail?
column2: Activities

column1: Name two works Rogers says went too far with weirdness.
column2: Any two of: Dune (1984), The City of Lost Children (1995), SkullMonkeys, Muscle Man March

column1: Who observed the three types of story audience?
column2: Ken Levine, director of Bioshock (2009 GDC talk)

column1: What are the three types of story audience?
column2: Into the story as it happens; want it in depth; don't care at all

column1: What's the rule of thumb for serving all three audiences?
column2: Story serves the gameplay, never the other way around.

column1: How did Bioshock and Batman: Arkham Asylum serve depth-seekers?
column2: Optional collectible audiotapes with deeper story details

column1: Why reveal story through gameplay and level design too?
column2: Many players skip cutscenes and audio cues; without it they get lost (love thy player).

column1: Screenwriters change plot or action about every ____ minutes.
When doesn't 'start late in the action' apply well?
column2: Games without a traditional story, like puzzle games such as Tetris.

column1: Why does Rogers defend predictable endings?
column2: Wish fulfillment (good guys win) and predicting outcomes makes players feel smart; the fun is in the how.

column1: With 1980s Bond films, Rogers knew the WHO, WHAT and WHY but not the ____.
column2: HOW

column1: What does Rogers call the #1 video game story cliché?
column2: Amnesia

column1: Why does Rogers consider amnesia plots unfair?
column2: They become an excuse for an unreliable narrator to withhold information for a shock ending.

column1: In Hitchcock's example, how long does the surprise explosion's shock last?
column2: About 15 seconds

column1: Why does suspense beat surprise, per Hitchcock?
column2: Showing the danger in advance makes the audience emotionally involved for the whole scene.

column1: Name the three games Rogers cites for themes beyond 'violence solves all problems'.
column2: Frogger, Zoo Tycoon, Braid

column1: What was a kill screen originally?
column2: A screen caused by a bug or oversight, not a designed game over (e.g., Pac-Man level 256)

column1: Which game made players want to know if the hero rescued the princess, giving birth to game story?
column2: Dragon's Lair (Dirk)

column1: What average game length does Rogers cite for 2010?
column2: 8–10 hours (vs about 20 in the old days and 40 in the really old days)

column1: When should a game end, according to Rogers?
column2: When the player feels satisfied and has accomplished everything they needed to (play fair).

column1: Name four kinds of extras that extend play after the story.
column2: Multiple endings, minigames, unlockable/downloadable content, deleted levels

column1: What are the four title types?
column2: Literal, action/cool, punny, purple cow

column1: What are the three sources of a literal title?
column2: Main character, main location, or a gameplay activity/component

column1: What's the risk of a punny title?
column2: The audience may not get the reference or find it funny; humor is subjective.

column1: What's the big advantage of a purple cow title?
column2: Once a word is linked to your game, others can't use it without evoking your game (e.g., Halo).

column1: Why are short titles better?
column2: Easier to remember and say, and easier to make into logos for start screens and boxes.

column1: Which single word does Rogers call one of the best game names ever?
column2: Defender

column1: Why name your game early?
column2: Otherwise the publisher's marketing department will name it for you.

column1: Per Andy Ashcraft, which act do developers mostly tell?
column2: The second act

column1: Why does the first act matter for characters?
column2: It's where players learn about and come to care about the character, so later events have impact.

column1: How would Rogers redesign the Robocop game opening?
column2: Level 1 plays as human cop Alex Murphy, ending with his death, before he becomes Robocop.

column1: Name three gameplay roles that make a character's loss felt.
column2: Teaching how to play, running the economy (shopkeeper), providing health power-ups

column1: Which game death does Rogers call the only truly impactful one?
column2: Aeris in Final Fantasy VII

column1: Where does humor come from, according to Rogers?
column2: Character: characters being true to themselves (e.g., Team Fortress 2)

column1: How did Maximo's personality shape his animations?
column2: He was impatient, so he kicked treasure chests open instead of opening them.

column1: List Rogers' eight character motivations.
column2: Success, revenge, love, acceptance, escape, hunger, responsibility, knowledge

column1: What lesson comes from Luke Skywalker's original name, Starkiller?
column2: Never give a character a name that gives away the ending.

column1: What's the rule of thumb for character names?
column2: When you look at the character's image, the name should fit what you see.

column1: What's the most common mistake in writing for kids?
column2: Making the story too simple

column1: What's the difference between licensor and licensee?
column2: Licensor owns the property; licensee pays a fee to use it in a game.

column1: What is a TV show 'bible'?
column2: A detailed document outlining the show's characters and worlds

column1: Why base public-domain games on the original material?
column2: Someone else's interpretation may be protected; the original is free.

column1: Your F2P event story is 4 screens of text before level 1. Which tip is broken?
column2: Start as late into the action as possible (and serve the skippers).

column1: Your concept has alien heroes, on an alien planet, doing an alien sport. What's the risk?
column2: It violates the Triangle of Weirdness: players won't get it. Make two corners familiar.

column1: You want players to feel tension in a limited-time event. Which idea fits?
column2: Hitchcock's suspense: show the danger in advance (visible timers, approaching threats).

column1: Your story kills the shopkeeper in chapter 1 and nobody cares. What went wrong?
column2: No first act or bond: invest time and make the character important to gameplay before the loss.

column1: A licensor forbids gacha mechanics after you built the economy. Which tip did you skip?
column2: Uncover the big issues (no-nos) early.

column1: Your brawler is a chef but fights with a sniper rifle. Which principle is broken?
column2: Profession should drive actions: give the chef kitchen-themed attacks.

column1: Your mobile game's name is 7 words long. What should you do?
column2: Shorten it (2–3 syllables ideal); store names have character limits and home screens truncate.

column1: Name the book's examples of action/cool titles and of punny titles.
column2: Action/cool: Darksiders, Brütal Legend, Gears of War. Punny: Just Cause, Half-Life, System Shock.

column1: Give the book's examples of literal titles by source (character, location, activity/component).
column2: Character: Sonic the Hedgehog, Voodoo Vince. Location: Castle Wolfenstein, Saints Row. Activity/component: Command & Conquer, Boom Blocks.

column1: Where does the term "purple cow" come from, and which titles does the book use as purple cows?
column2: A poem by Gelett Burgess about never having seen a purple cow. Titles: LittleBigPlanet, Far Cry, Resident Evil (and Halo, a word now tied to its game).

column1: By roughly which page of the Robocop script do we care about Alex Murphy?
column2: About page 25: honest cop in futuristic Detroit, so his shooting hurts before he becomes the cyborg.

column1: Give Rogers' three reasons the Robocop games started you as Robocop.
column2: (1) A criminal-blasting cyborg is more appealing than a fragile human. (2) 1988 cartridges lacked memory for two different player models. (3) The title is Robocop.

column1: In Rogers' Little Red Riding Hood game, why can't you kill the wolf at the first encounter?
column2: It is the first enemy encounter and the wolf is the eventual boss, unless the early enemies are "wolf minions".

column1: What does Hitchcock add about the characters in the bomb-under-the-table scene, and why does it matter for games?
column2: Don't actually kill them; in a game that would be game over.

column1: Why must designers craft pacing by hand if they have no Left 4 Dead style Director?
column2: Most developers lack that technology, so it is up to the designer to build those paced, emotional situations as best they can.

column1: How did arcade owners recover from the Pac-Man level-256 kill screen?
column2: Half the screen turns to garbled data so the board can't be cleared; owners had to unplug ("kill") the machine and restart it.

column1: Match the licensors to their properties: Lucasfilm, DC Comics, J.K. Rowling, Nickelodeon.
column2: Lucasfilm: Star Wars. DC Comics: Batman. J.K. Rowling: Harry Potter. Nickelodeon: SpongeBob SquarePants.

column1: Which public-domain properties does Rogers list, and what is the caveat?
column2: Dracula, Dante's Inferno, Cinderella, The Three Musketeers, The Wizard of Oz, The Bible. Base your game on the original material, not someone else's interpretation.

column1: Which name pairs does Rogers use as examples of juxtaposed names and of comedic names?
column2: Juxtaposed: Harry Burns (curmudgeonly) and Sally Allbright (positive, naive) from When Harry Met Sally. Comedic: Guybrush Threepwood, SpongeBob SquarePants, Larry Laffer.

column1: What did a childhood Batman comic teach Rogers, and what point does that prove?
column2: African masks, 1920s comedians, the opera Pagliacci and how paraffin wax changes color over the years: entertainment can teach without feeling like edutainment.

column1: Which Team Fortress 2 characters does Rogers use to show humor from character?
column2: The wry Australian sniper who defends his job to his parents and the Russian heavy who loves his "sanviches"; looks, animations and voice barks all reinforce their personalities.

column1: At GDC, which game does each side shout in the story vs gameplay fight?
column2: Pro-story designers shout Bioshock; anti-story designers shout Doom.

column1: What does each camp in the story vs gameplay debate claim?
column2: Pro-story: games need a story to engage players and are an artistic medium for telling stories. Anti-story: story is how people describe play afterward, or what you watch while the game loads.

column1: What are the four preproduction documents, in order?
column2: One-sheet, ten-pager, beat chart, game design document (GDD).

column1: What do all four preproduction documents eventually evolve into?
column2: The game design document (GDD).

column1: How long do many GDDs average, according to Rogers?
column2: Over 300 pages, though it isn't a fixed number.

column1: What is Rogers' rule for how long a GDD should be?
column2: Just long enough to accurately describe what's going on in the game.

column1: How does Mark Cerny format his design material?
column2: One page per topic, in bullet points.

column1: What is the goal of design documentation?
column2: Communication: with the player, the team and publishing partners.

column1: Why must a one-sheet fit on a single page?
column2: Many busy people (teammates, publishers) read it, so it has to be short as well as interesting and informative.

column1: What are the eight fields of Rogers' one-sheet?
column2: Title, game systems, target age, intended ESRB rating, story summary focused on gameplay, distinct modes, USPs, competitive products.

column1: Besides ratings, what does the ESRB enforce?
column2: Advertising and online-privacy principles, for the US and Canada.

column1: Which rating system do the ESRB's letter ratings most resemble?
column2: The MPAA movie ratings (G, PG, PG-13, R, X).

column1: Name three non-US rating systems mentioned in the book.
column2: PEGI (Europe), BBFC (UK), USK (Germany).

column1: What were the six ESRB ratings in 2010?
Why did the eC rating carry stigma?
column2: Gamers saw it as 'baby games', since it mostly appeared on edutainment and licensed titles for young kids.

column1: Why did publishers avoid the AO rating?
column2: No US brick-and-mortar retailer would stock an AO game; it was the industry's X rating.

column1: What are comps?
column2: Already-released games similar to yours, listed to help readers understand your game quickly.

column1: Why should comps be successful or very familiar games?
column2: Publishers know sales figures, and comparing your game to a flop can scare them off.

column1: Rogers recommends about ____ USPs.
column2: five

column1: Why about five USPs?
column2: That's roughly how many bullet points fit on the back of a game box.

column1: Name three phrases that don't count as USPs.
column2: 'Amazing graphics', 'awesome story', 'sequel to an award-winning game'.

column1: What is a ten-pager?
column2: A broad-strokes design document that lays out the game's spine without excruciating detail.

column1: Why build a ten-pager in PowerPoint or similar?
column2: It helps formatting, and you can present it on screen in a pitch or print it as a leave-behind.

column1: What does the production team want from a ten-pager?
column2: Clear gameplay diagrams, short punchy sentences, specific terminology, and comparisons to appropriate games, even old ones.

column1: What do marketing and executives want from a ten-pager?
column2: Exciting concept images, bullet points, vivid examples, and successful modern games as comps.

column1: What five items go on the Ten-Pager title page?
column2: Title, game systems, target age, intended ESRB rating, projected ship date.

column1: Why make a placeholder logo with a carefully chosen font for the ten-pager?
column2: The font tells readers the genre instantly, without needing pictures.

column1: What are the two parts of Ten-Pager Page 2 (game outline)?
column2: The game story summary and the game flow.

column1: What questions should the game flow answer?
column2: What the challenges are and how to overcome them; how progression and rewards work; how gameplay ties to the story; what the victory condition is.

column1: God of War's team described Kratos with one word that shaped all his actions: ____.
column2: Brutal

column1: What diagram must Ten-Pager Page 5 (game world) include?
column2: A simple map or flowchart showing how the player navigates the world.

column1: Gestalt translates as ____.
column2: 'the whole' (the overall feel of the complete experience)

column1: Why should Page 6 include a flowchart of the game's shell (menus)?
column2: Many games have lousy interfaces because the team never thought about them.

column1: What is a mechanic?
column2: Something the player interacts with to create or aid gameplay (moving platforms, doors, rope swings, ice).

column1: What is a hazard?
column2: A mechanic that can harm or kill the player but has no intelligence.

column1: A hazard that uses artificial intelligence is an ____.
column2: enemy

column1: What's the difference between a power-up and a collectible?
column2: A power-up helps gameplay directly; a collectible has no immediate gameplay effect but may buy or unlock things later.

column1: How many mechanics does Rogers say to describe at the ten-pager stage?
column2: About three.

column1: What questions should the ten-pager answer about each boss?
column2: Who they are, where they appear, how they're defeated, and what the player earns.

column1: What does Ten-Pager Page 10 cover?
column2: Bonus materials and unlockables that encourage replay: multiplayer, DLC, episodic content.

column1: How does a game bible differ from a GDD?
column2: The bible covers world rules and character backgrounds and relationships; the GDD covers gameplay.

column1: If nobody reads the GDD, why write it?
column2: You'll need it yourself; keeping the game in your head leads to overwhelm and forgotten ideas.

column1: What are Rogers' five techniques for communicating a design?
column2: Storyboards, diagrams, animatics, beat charts, the team wiki.

column1: Why is a team wiki risky?
column2: Once preproduction becomes production, the design team tends to neglect it and it goes out of date.

column1: Why should gameplay diagrams use consistent shapes and colors plus a legend?
column2: So readers know what each icon and shape means and read the diagram the same way.

column1: 'Everything is ____' means your design will change during production.
column2: liquid

column1: Who are the GDD's four primary readers?
column2: The producer, designer, artist and programmer.

column1: What does Rogers call the most important part of a game designer's job?
column2: Communication.

column1: What term did Rogers invent to replace 'robots' for the Zin?
column2: Clockwork undead.

column1: Why do vague words like 'robot' cause problems in a GDD?
column2: Each teammate pictures something different (C-3PO vs the Iron Giant), so the team ends up on different pages.

column1: What is 'progression'?
column2: How the gameplay unfolds for the player over the course of the game.

column1: What are the five ways to start a game's progression?
column2: Ground zero; skills shown but unlocked over time; skills without knowing how to use them; big power then lost; big power then back to zero via a flashback.

column1: Which story cliché does Rogers say to avoid unless you're exceptionally clever?
column2: The hero with amnesia (and 'it was all a dream').

column1: A beat chart has ____ required elements per level.
What is 'clumping' in a beat chart?
column2: Introducing too many new enemies or mechanics at once.

column1: What is 'samey-ness'?
column2: Too many identical combinations of enemies and mechanics.

column1: By what point should the player have everything?
column2: About 75% of the way through the game.

column1: Why give the player everything by about 75%?
column2: So the last quarter lets them play with all their cool stuff.

column1: Rogers’ rule of thumb: introduce ____ new mechanics, enemies and rewards per level.
column2: two or three

column1: What minimum gameplay time does Rogers advise for action games?
column2: 8–10 hours, not counting replays, cutscenes or dialogue.

column1: What is 'not invented here' syndrome?
column2: Believing that ideas from anyone outside the design team aren't valid.

column1: Why tackle the tough design problems first?
column2: If they don't work out, there's still time to change course.

column1: What date format does Rogers prefer for documents?
column2: Day, month as text, year (e.g., 27 JUL 09).

column1: What is IARC?
column2: The International Age Rating Coalition: one questionnaire generates regional age ratings (used by Google Play and other stores).

column1: What are Apple's App Store age tiers after the 2025 update?
Which ESRB notices matter most for F2P games?
column2: 'In-Game Purchases' (2018) and 'In-Game Purchases (Includes Random Items)' (2020).

column1: Your event spec just says 'players get a reward', and QA, art and economy each picture something different. Which principle applies?
column2: Be specific with words (the 'clockwork undead' rule): name the exact rewards and amounts and keep a glossary.

column1: Level 31 of your puzzle game introduces two new blockers and a booster at once, and its win rate crashes. Which beat-chart warning is this?
column2: Clumping. Spread new elements out (2–3 per level at most; on mobile, one blocker at a time) and introduce each with its counter.

column1: Your pitch lists eight comps, including a recent flop. What two rules are you breaking?
column2: The Rule of Threes (use three examples) and 'always pick a winning horse' (successful or very familiar comps).

column1: Your store screenshot caption says 'Stunning graphics!' What's wrong with it?
column2: It isn't a USP. Every game claims it. Replace it with a unique feature you can show.

column1: Executives ask why the game will make money, while the team asks how the event works. How should the deck handle both?
column2: Use the ten-pager audience split: a KPI and market page for executives, diagrams and rules for the team, all in one document.

column1: The team rewrites the event rules every sprint and morale is dropping. Which schmuck rule applies?
column2: Make a decision and stick with it. Work it out on paper first, and change direction only on evidence.

column1: Late in production, your team wants to add paid loot boxes. Which Universal Truth should you raise?
column2: Know your target rating and design toward it: random-item descriptors, odds disclosure and regional rules all apply.

column1: Players unlock the best hero in the final chapter and never get to use it. Which beat-chart guideline does this break?
column2: Give players everything by about 75% (in F2P, give every new tool a stretch of play before the next gate).

column1: Your LiveOps calendar runs the same race event every weekend for ten weeks. Which beat-chart problem is this?
column2: Samey-ness. Alternate event types and themes.

column1: A stale wiki spec caused the wrong reward values to ship. Which warning came true, and what's the fix?
column2: Wiki rot (the team wiki going out of date). Fix: one owner per page, status labels, a changelog, frequent updates.

column1: Marketing needs screenshots of a boss at level 200 by tomorrow. Which rule would have saved you?
column2: Be prepared: level skips, a cheat camera, debug and cheat menus.

column1: A new FTUE lets players fight with a maxed-out team, then resets them to starter heroes. Which of Rogers' progression starts is this?
column2: Significant power right away, then lost after the first confrontation.

column1: You're pitching a puzzle game with no main character. What should Page 2 emphasize instead?
column2: The environments and places the levels represent (like Peggle's Peggle Masters), told vividly.

column1: Rogers' motto for choosing comps: always pick a ____.
column2: winning horse

column1: What do all of Rogers' sample USPs have in common?
column2: Each is a single line with a concrete number or name plus a hook (256-player co-op, 1,000+ tunes, 200 levels, named weapons, a named engine) and no lengthy detail.

column1: In Rogers' sample USP list, the co-op mode supports ____ players, the soundtrack has over ____ tunes, and the open world has ____ levels.
Name the three signature weapons in Rogers' sample USP list, and the Rule of Threes link.
column2: The blastinator, the skull-defiler and the fire-ant anguisher: three named examples in one bullet, with the engine named Realitech in another.

column1: What does Maximo 1-2 drop compared with 1-1 on the beat chart?
column2: The wooden coffin and chest mimic enemies; breakable rocks and the cave gate; the Achille statue, fall-away ground, breakaway bridge and deep water hazards; the iron key; and the 'foot cheese' ability (swapped for throw shield).

column1: Why compare beat-chart columns for what a level drops as well as what it adds?
column2: Drops show how the level rotates its hazard set (water and bridges out, fire and a swinging gate in) while the core kit stays, keeping a mastery level fresh without clumping.

column1: Who is the villain behind the drill in Maximo 1-2's story, and where else does his name appear on the chart?
column2: Achille. His name is already on 1-1's key statue (mechanic) and statue (hazard).

column1: What five things does Rogers' one-sentence Tomb Raider: Legend game-flow example convey?
column2: Who you play (Lara Croft), camera (third person), genre (action-adventure), locations (Bolivia's jungles to Tibet's mountains) and goals (find the Ghalali key, solve the mystery of Lara's lost mother).

column1: What are Rogers' Three Cs?
column2: Character, Camera, Control.

column1: What is the 'very important rule' of character design?
column2: Form follows function: a character's actions and personality determine their appearance.

column1: Rogers' three personality traits for Mario?
column2: Courageous, bouncy, happy.

column1: Rogers' three personality traits for Sonic?
column2: Fast, cool, edgy.

column1: Rogers' three personality traits for Kratos?
column2: Brutal, vicious, selfish.

column1: What do circles communicate in character design?
column2: Friendliness.

column1: What do squares communicate in character design?
column2: Strength or dumbness, depending on how big the square is.

column1: What does a point-down triangle mean as a body vs as a head?
column2: As a body: a heroic, powerful frame. As a head: sinister.

column1: Four benefits of a strong silhouette?
column2: Shows personality at a glance, tells characters apart, marks friend vs enemy, stands out against the background.

column1: Which game does Rogers use to show gameplay-ready silhouettes?
column2: Team Fortress 2 (Heavy vs Pyro vs Spy, etc.).

column1: Rogers' three types of video game character?
column2: Humorous, heroic and badass (anti-hero).

column1: Three rules for a heroic character?
column2: Does heroic things that matter; is good at something (a specialty); isn't perfect (relatable flaws, ideally used in gameplay).

column1: Three rules for a badass character?
column2: Does everything with style; isn't nice (enjoys it); says cool things but almost never shouts.

column1: How did Maximo vs. Army of Zin make players feel heroic?
column2: Optional rescues of menaced villagers with small rewards and no penalty for skipping.

column1: What did X-Com: UFO Defense teach Rogers?
column2: Renaming soldiers made him care about them. Customization creates attachment.

column1: The six customization categories Rogers lists?
column2: Name, appearance, clothing/armor/gear, vehicles, home base, weapons.

column1: What should never be customizable?
column2: The signature weapon/gear/look. It's part of the character's identity.

column1: Why do Lara's ponytail and Batman's cape exist, design-wise?
column2: Heroes are mostly seen from behind and need something that shows movement.

column1: What is the uncanny valley?
column2: A near-realistic character that looks subtly wrong to viewers, which is distracting (especially in cutscenes).

column1: Rogers' three tips for realistic characters?
column2: Avoid exaggerated facial features; invest in movement and rigging (stiff shoulders, ham hands); human-looking characters will be expected to act human.

column1: What measurement unit did Rogers' team use on Maximo?
column2: '1 Maximo unit', based on the hero's height and width.

column1: Rogers' jump height rule of thumb?
column2: A jump is about ½ the hero's height; a double jump up to 2× the hero's height.

column1: How does jump distance compare with walk and run?
column2: Farther than a walk, not as far as a run (or set in hero widths, e.g. 5 units).

column1: How much height does a hoist add?
column2: Up to a full body length on top of the jump height.

column1: Which single collision point does Rogers prefer?
column2: The torso (center of the body).

column1: The five phases of a jump?
column2: At rest; instant takeoff; quick rise (double jump before apex); short, non-floaty fall; landing that sticks.

column1: Rogers' five types of jump?
column2: Single, double, triple, contextual, wall jump.

column1: What is the 'jump zone'?
column2: The area players take off from: up to half a jump's distance back from the edge.

column1: Where do players aim to land after a jump?
column2: A safe spot roughly half a jump's length in from the far edge (dead center on small platforms).

column1: What is a 'hang'?
column2: Being in the hoist position without having climbed up or dropped down.

column1: What is the Wile E. Coyote effect?
column2: A character visibly standing or hanging on thin air at an edge.

column1: Name four benefits of a character's shadow.
column2: 3D reference for jumps, grounding (weight and mass), edge detection, lighting and mood, stealth AI use (and, jokingly, a soul).

column1: What is a drop shadow?
column2: A simple dark spot under the character that shows exactly where they are and where they'll land.

column1: Rogers' rule for water in one environment?
column2: It's all safe or all deadly. 'No deep end to the pool.'

column1: What is a dash cooldown, and how long is it typically?
column2: A wait before the dash can be reused, usually a few seconds, to prevent exploits.

column1: What is 'player zapping'?
column2: Resident Evil 0's name for switching between SPCs. Keep it to one button press.

column1: Four ways to choose between several SPCs?
column2: Nearest character, cycle a preset list, compass-style direct-select window, auto-switch at a set level location.

column1: What's the difference between an SPC and a companion?
column2: An SPC is a second playable character you can control (AI-run when you don't). A companion is always run by the game's AI.

column1: Which pair shows 'opposites attract' companions?
column2: Resident Evil 2's Claire (fighter, two guns) and Sherry (defenseless, crawls into hiding spots for puzzle items).

column1: What question must every NPC answer?
column2: What does the player need to succeed?

column1: What is NPC 'business'?
column2: Background activity (eating, chatting, chopping wood) that makes the world look alive, like film extras.

column1: How did Bioshock help players tell NPCs apart?
column2: By giving them strong international accents (distinct 'voices').

column1: Why must the Three Cs be locked early?
column2: So many systems depend on them that changes ripple into rework and broken gameplay, and can even cancel a game.

column1: Why is a stoic badass risky?
column2: Stoicism can easily read as having no personality.

column1: Why reward rather than force good deeds?
column2: Preaching is bad form. Optional, rewarded good deeds let players feel heroic by their own choice.

column1: Why let players name their characters?
column2: Naming and customization create ownership, and ownership creates caring (the X-Com lesson).

column1: Why are metrics so important to players?
column2: Players judge reachable distances by eye. Breaking learned constants feels wrong.

column1: Why is head-based collision a problem?
column2: Ground collision makes the character look unrooted, slightly floating.

column1: Why is feet-based collision bad for pickups?
column2: Pickups floating in mid-air would force the player to jump to collect them.

column1: Why is walking not gameplay?
column2: Long travel is boring regardless of art. Players prefer faster, varied moves and don't love collecting as much as designers love placing.

column1: Why must a jump start instantly?
column2: Many jumps are reactions to danger, so any delay feels unresponsive.

column1: Why shouldn't falls last long?
column2: They feel floaty, which is unpleasant and breaks the player's sense of metrics (unless gliding is a power).

column1: Why add an extra jump length to gap designs?
column2: Players take off from back from the edge and aim well inside the far edge, because edges make them nervous.

column1: Why save tiny platforms for late in the game?
column2: Nervous players re-jump and overshoot to their deaths. Tiny targets belong in expert challenges.

column1: Why must hang and teeter animations loop?
column2: Players may leave the hero hanging or teetering indefinitely.

column1: Why do quadrupeds need special metrics?
column2: Wider turning radius, faster acceleration, longer bodies hanging over edges, shorter height for attacks and doors.

column1: Why are companions so costly to make?
column2: They need sophisticated AI and animation quality on par with the main character's.

column1: Why start a big cast from stereotypes?
column2: Without story, players pick by looks. Archetypes read instantly, then gameplay makes each unique.

column1: Why keep character stats easy to edit?
column2: So global balance changes don't take endless manual tweaking.

column1: Your stealth game stars a giant axe-wielding barbarian, and players keep charging in and dying. What went wrong?
column2: Mixed signals: form must follow function. A stealth hero should look and act stealthy.

column1: Runner players complain they miss coins at chest height. What collision fix fits?
column2: Use torso-centered, generous pickup collision instead of feet-based detection.

column1: Playtesters keep trying to jump to a ledge you meant to be unreachable. Fix?
column2: Make it visibly higher than double the hero's height (or add a hoist if it should be reachable).

column1: Your level doc says 'the player walks down the long corridor to the boss.' Which principle?
column2: Walking is NOT gameplay. Add varied traversal or cut the corridor.

column1: Your dash is being spammed in PvP. What does Rogers recommend?
column2: Add a cooldown, usually a few seconds.

column1: One pond in your level is safe, the next deadly. What's the problem?
column2: There's no deep end to the pool. Use one water rule per environment, or give strong warnings.

column1: A +5 sword upgrade isn't exciting players. How do you fix it?
column2: Make it visible (glow, flame, runes, extra bits) or change the hero's stance and animation.

column1: Two brawlers in your roster have nearly identical stat rows. Which tool flags this?
column2: The abilities matrix. No two characters should share specs; differentiate one or sell it as a skin.

column1: Players call your AI companion useless and annoying. What principle should guide the redesign?
column2: Opposites attract: give her complementary abilities players need, and build the relationship early.

column1: An NPC in your game only says 'nice weather today.' What's missing?
column2: A job. Every NPC must answer 'what does the player need to succeed?'

column1: Your realistic hero looks creepy in cutscenes. What are your options?
column2: Uncanny valley: fix facial proportions and rigging, or switch to a stylized look (as TF2 did).

column1: Players land jumps and then slide off platforms. Fix?
column2: Remove post-landing skids/slides. Landings should 'stick'.

column1: Players die in pits they couldn't see while jumping. Rule?
column2: Let players see the death zone. No blind leaps of faith.

column1: A new premium skin hides the hero's signature weapon and changes the silhouette. What's the risk?
column2: Lost identity and battlefield readability. Keep the signature item and silhouette recognizable.

column1: Your FTUE mascot keeps explaining swipes after players have mastered them. Which rule is broken?
column2: Never tell the player something they already know.

column1: Form follows ____.
column2: function

column1: Walking is NOT ____!
column2: gameplay

column1: A jump is about ____ the hero's height; a double jump up to ____ it.
column2: half; twice

column1: Let players double jump before the ____ of the first jump.
column2: apex

column1: Players take off from the '____', up to half a jump from the edge.
column2: jump zone

column1: There is no ____ to the pool.
column2: deep end

column1: Every player likes to play ____.
column2: house

column1: What four things does your camera choice affect?
column2: How the camera is programmed, how the game is designed, how controls are mapped, how art is created.

column1: How many 'main' camera styles should a game have?
column2: One main style for most of the gameplay. Others only for specific situations.

column1: Define a static camera.
column2: A camera that never moves and stays fixed on a single screen, location and image.

column1: Why does art for a static camera cost less?
column2: Objects seen from only one angle don't need a back, which saves production and processing time.

column1: What is the main danger of a static screen, and the fix?
column2: It isn't dynamic. Compensate with lots of animation and effects.

column1: Which survival horror games used static cameras to set mood?
column2: Alone in the Dark and Resident Evil.

column1: What two advantages does a scrollable camera add over a static one?
column2: The engaging act of moving the camera, and the ability to hide things off screen and reveal them dramatically.

column1: What are a camera's 'hydraulics'?
column2: Its acceleration and deceleration speed.

column1: Why is a scrollable camera that moves too fast frustrating?
column2: It overshoots the target and the player corrects back and forth.

column1: If you let players set scroll speed, what two rules apply?
column2: Make the option easy to find, and offer several speeds (not just fast/slow).

column1: Which company introduced parallax scrolling in 1982?
column2: Irem (with its moon-buggy game, Moon Patrol).

column1: What testing tip goes with plain parallax scrolling?
column2: Play the level backwards to make sure the player can't outrun the load and break the game.

column1: What is a forced scroll camera?
column2: A camera that moves on its own. The player must keep up or something horrible (like death) happens.

column1: Why shouldn't you use forced scrolling throughout a game?
column2: It's exhausting pressure. Use it for moments, unless the whole game is built on the idea.

column1: Why is level design for Mode 7 tricky?
column2: The level has no real far wall, so the illusion only holds over a background that never ends.

column1: Which game used a multi-plane camera for bi-dimensional gameplay, the forerunner of 2.5D?
column2: Disney's Hercules Action Game (Virgin Interactive, 1997).

column1: Which two games popularized the first-person camera?
column2: Wolfenstein 3D (1992) and Doom (1993).

column1: Name the four disadvantages of the first-person camera.
column2: Hard to judge jumps and distances; can't see the character (weaker emotional link); player may not look where the designer wants; pickups must be exaggerated in scale.

column1: Why does Rogers dislike heavy screen darkening for dying players?
column2: It unfairly adds a second penalty by hiding the gameplay and where damage comes from.

column1: What must 'Predator vision' effects provide besides looking cool?
column2: A real gameplay advantage.

column1: What does DIMS stand for?
column2: Doom-Induced Motion Sickness.

column1: Why does DIMS happen?
column2: The eyes register movement but the inner ear (balance) doesn't feel it.

column1: Name Rogers' six designer remedies for DIMS.
column2: ~60 fps; no bobbing foreground (weapon); flat floors; large stationary focus objects; don't whip the camera; limit fast or frequent up/down looking.

column1: Why does a third-person camera reduce DIMS somewhat?
column2: The character gives the player something stable to focus on.

column1: What is 'sorting'?
column2: When the camera passes through a character or geometry, often revealing the sky or background color.

column1: Where should the 'turn objects transparent' fix for sorting NOT be used?
column2: On perimeter walls. It works for objects inside the walls.

column1: Why shouldn't objects disappear completely when the camera gets close?
column2: Things flickering in and out of existence disorient players (and look bad).

column1: What is camera flipping and its number one cause?
column2: The camera bouncing between objects while trying to settle. Corners cause it most.

column1: How should you keep players out of corners?
column2: Visible blocking geometry (retaining walls, shrubs, boulders, fences), never invisible walls. Keep collectables and AI paths out of corners.

column1: Which follow-cam position does Rogers prefer, and why?
column2: Laid back (loose follow): fewer obstructions, you see the hero's face, enemies can sneak up behind, chases are easier.

column1: What are the three methods for giving players camera control?
column2: Full 360 follow-cam control, free-look camera, selective control.

column1: How does selective control differ from free-look?
column2: Context: free-look simulates turning your head; selective simulates equipment (scope, binoculars) and should share its limits.

column1: Why are some free-look cameras limited to just under 180 degrees?
column2: To mimic the natural rotation of the human neck.

column1: What camera trick does Rogers use when the player stops moving?
column2: Slightly overshoot the target, then creep back to center if the player stays still.

column1: What was Resident Evil 4's solution to the jarring third-to-first-person switch?
column2: When aiming, the camera shifts to hover behind the character's shoulder.

column1: What is second person view? Give an example.
column2: The camera is given to a different character. Mark of Kri's bird Kuzo, or The Darkness's tentacle cam.

column1: Why did God of War build environments like theater sets?
column2: With a designer-controlled camera, unseen sides never need to be built, which saves polygons and textures.

column1: What is the most important rule when removing camera control?
column2: Make it clear to the player that they don't have control.

column1: What two things should you never do behind an obstruction that hides the character?
column2: Place hazards there, or widen the path (allowing Z-axis movement).

column1: How does 2.5D differ from bi-dimensional gameplay?
column2: 2.5D uses 3D models but 2D-style camera limits. Bi-dimensional uses sprites.

column1: Which game introduced the isometric camera?
column2: Zaxxon (Sega, 1982).

column1: Why can elevation be confusing in an isometric view?
column2: High-and-near and low-and-far objects can appear in the same screen spot.
