column1: What is God view?
column2: An isometric camera with a much wider field of view (up to 'low orbit'), for controlling cities or land masses.

column1: What should be avoided in top-down views?
column2: Depth-based concepts. You also can't see the character or world well.

column1: Where should a swimming player's camera be?
column2: Underwater with the player, unless they swim at the surface. Keep 'in water' and 'on land' distinct, and don't bob.

column1: Why use a rail camera in caves and sewers?
column2: It avoids camera problems in tight spaces and keeps the feeling of claustrophobia.

column1: What does a medium close up (MCU) show, and when is it used?
column2: Head and shoulders, mostly for talking characters. Animate the hands.

column1: What's the difference between a cutaway and a cut in?
column2: Cutaway: cut to the thing mentioned or a reaction. Cut in: cut to a close-up detail of what's being examined.

column1: What is a 'noddy' shot?
column2: A character reacting (nodding) to someone else speaking.

column1: What does a low camera angle do to a subject?
column2: Makes it look menacing or impressive, great for bosses.

column1: What is a dolly zoom?
column2: Changing focal length while moving the camera so the subject stays the same size and the background warps.

column1: Pedestal vs tilt?
column2: Pedestal physically moves the camera up. Tilt aims the camera up or down while its position stays fixed.

column1: Extreme wide shot, very wide shot, wide shot, medium shot, ____, close up, extreme close up.
column2: Medium close up (MCU)

column1: The #1 cause of camera flipping is ____.
column2: corners

column1: Rule of thirds: put the focus item a ____ of the way up or across the screen.
column2: third

column1: Treat the camera like it's the player's ____.
column2: spotter

column1: Scenario: your match-3 board looks lifeless in playtests. Which static-camera rule applies?
column2: Static screens aren't dynamic. Compensate with lots of animation and effects (juice).

column1: Scenario: players in your base builder fling the map and keep overshooting their buildings. What do you tune?
column2: The camera's hydraulics (acceleration/deceleration, inertia and friction), and maybe offer speed settings.

column1: Scenario: in your top-down brawler, the hero vanishes behind tall walls. Name two fixes.
column2: Fade the walls or draw a ghost outline of the hero through them (also gaps in geometry, arrows).

column1: Scenario: a cutscene shows the hero running right, then the next shot shows him running left. What rule was broken?
column2: Crossing the line (180° rule). Add a front-on shot or keep cameras on one side.

column1: Scenario: you want a gacha hero reveal to feel powerful. Which angle and movement?
column2: A low angle plus an arc (360 orbit) around the hero.

column1: Scenario: playtesters say a screen 'feels broken' because they keep trying to drag it. Which camera rule?
column2: If players don't control the camera, make that clear. Don't make a screen look draggable when it isn't.

column1: Scenario: your 4X game needs a view of the whole continent. Which camera?
column2: God view: isometric with a very wide field of view.

column1: Scenario: your runner's player can sprint faster than chunks load on cheap phones. What does Rogers advise?
column2: Watch for 'outrunning the load'. Test by playing the level backwards and at max speed to try to break it.

column1: Scenario: players miss the level goal in your puzzle game. Which principle?
column2: Always point the camera to the objective. Show the goal at level start. Chekhov's gun.

column1: Why is isometric popular for base-building games?
column2: Its toy-like view plus quick reads of layout and item relationships make planning easy and the base look like a toy.

column1: Scenario: your third-person mobile game camera keeps jittering between two walls when players collect a corner chest. What's the cleanest fix?
column2: Move the chest out of the corner (keep gameplay mid-room). If it must stay, raise the camera up the wall to an angled bird's-eye view.

column1: Scenario: the scope in your mobile shooter has a perfect 360° view with zero sway. Which rule does this ignore?
column2: Selective control should mirror the real equipment's limits. Realism sells the view.

column1: Scenario: your underwater bonus level bobs the camera to feel realistic and testers feel queasy. What do you change?
column2: Remove the bobbing (it causes DIMS) and keep the camera submerged with the player.

column1: Scenario: you want your F2P art budget focused only on what players see. Which camera choice enables 'theater set' art?
column2: A designer-controlled (locked) camera, since unseen sides never need building.

column1: Scenario: a co-op mode keeps losing track of the second player when they run ahead. Name two options from the book.
column2: Zoom out to fit both (with off-screen arrows) or use split screen (possibly only when far apart). Camera in picture is a third.

column1: Scenario: you're adding a night-vision booster to a hidden-object game. What test must it pass?
column2: It must give a real gameplay advantage (reveal hidden things), not just look cool.

column1: Plain parallax tip: always play your level ____ to make sure players can't outrun the load.
column2: backwards

column1: DIMS stands for Doom-Induced ____ ____.
column2: Motion Sickness

column1: Isometric with a much wider field of view, up to 'low orbit', is called ____ view.
column2: God

column1: Why use a high camera angle for puzzle and strategy boards?
column2: High angles show elements in relationship to each other, which makes planning clear.

column1: Why should top-down games avoid depth-based challenges?
column2: From straight above, height and depth are hard to read, so jumps or vertical puzzles become guesswork.

column1: Where does the name 'Mode 7' come from?
column2: It is named after the 7th (out of 8) background layer of the Super Nintendo, the one used for the scaled, perspective ground plane.

column1: What lesson did Rogers take from the 'holding the controller wrong' story?
column2: Always remember that humans play these games, so design controls ergonomically.

column1: How did the 'holding it wrong' QTE story end?
column2: Three months later, playtesting showed the QTE was too hard and the controls were adjusted.

column1: Define ergonomics.
column2: The study of fitting equipment to the worker (or player).

column1: On the Flex-O-Fingering chart, what is the thumb's role?
column2: Primary control and primary response: flexible, good for steering and fast response (recommended).

column1: On the Flex-O-Fingering chart, what is the index finger's role?
column2: Primary trigger, primary hold, secondary response: strong and fast (recommended).

column1: How should the middle finger be used, per the chart?
column2: Secondary hold or trigger. Usable for hold moves but weaker, so use it infrequently.

column1: Why are the ring and pinkie fingers 'not recommended' for controls?
column2: They're weak with poor reach. They're better for stabilizing and supporting the grip.

column1: Why set control rules based on hand placement?
column2: It clarifies what goes where, and players build muscle memory linking movements to actions.

column1: What keyboard groupings does Rogers recommend clustering controls around?
column2: Common groupings like the QWERTY area and the WASD cluster. Don't use every key.

column1: How did Tak and the Guardians of Gross assign controls thematically?
column2: Wii Remote motion = all magic powers. Analog stick/nunchuk = real-world abilities (interacting, fighting).

column1: What's the danger with thematic control assignment?
column2: Crossing signals by mixing themes across inputs, which causes confusion.

column1: What are Rogers' control tips for younger players?
column2: Simple presses, no complex combos, and keyboard commands kept close together (kids hunt and peck).

column1: Besides power users, who benefits from customizable controls?
column2: Disabled gamers. Customization is accessibility-friendly.

column1: What was the 'pencil trick'?
column2: Rolling a pencil across buttons to mash fast enough in Track and Field (1983). It destroyed controllers.

column1: Why does Rogers call the pencil trick unfair?
column2: Players shouldn't have to resort to physical workarounds, which wreck hardware, to play your game.

column1: If you try an unconventional control scheme, what must you also offer?
column2: An option to revert to a traditional scheme (ideally several options or full remapping).

column1: Which way should pulling back on a flight stick move a plane?
column2: Up. Pull back = climb, push forward = dive. Don't reverse flight controls.

column1: What is the 'dance of the buttons'?
column2: An uncomplicated, non-repetitive scheme where fingers flow naturally between inputs.

column1: What is button mashing?
column2: Wildly or rapidly hitting random buttons because you don't know how to control the game, hoping for any result.

column1: What two causes of button mashing does Rogers name?
column2: A control scheme that's too complex, or unsatisfying feedback.

column1: What is 'gamers' thumb' and its symptoms?
column2: Occupational overuse syndrome: stiffness, burning or cold sensations, numbness or weakness.

column1: How often does the APTA advice say to stretch?
column2: Every 20 minutes (head, neck and shoulders).

column1: Why do new players press every button?
column2: They want to see what happens, and nobody reads the manual.

column1: How does God of War use button mashing to teach?
column2: Kratos does cool moves even when you mash. Players then slow down to learn how they did them.

column1: What are the three ways to make sure a button never does nothing?
column2: Negative response; mark inactive in training and celebrate the unlock; assign a redundant related function.

column1: What did the hero of Dark Castle do as a negative response?
column2: Shrugged when out of ammo or missing a key.

column1: What two cautions go with celebrating new move unlocks?
column2: Teach only one new move at a time, and don't introduce them too quickly. Overloaded players tune out.

column1: Why assign melee to the button a future projectile will use?
column2: The player links that button with combat before the true move unlocks, and the button is never dead.

column1: How does Pitfall: The Lost Expedition map the canteen?
column2: Push the stick forward at a cistern to fill, pull back to drink and restore health.

column1: In Maximo, why is jump on the X button?
column2: X is the lowest button on the pad, and the jump starts from the ground.

column1: In Maximo, why is shield throw on circle?
column2: The circle icon matches the round shield.

column1: Why copy the control scheme of successful games in your genre?
column2: Familiarity relieves confusion, so players embrace the game faster.

column1: Which functions belong on big triggers vs small shoulder buttons?
column2: Triggers: quick moves (shoot, brake, accelerate, melee). Small buttons: slow moves (precision aim, map, inventory).

column1: Why put quick moves on the bigger triggers?
column2: In the heat of action, fingers can slip off small buttons.

column1: When the player presses jump, the game should ask only ____.
column2: 'How high?'

column1: Where should beautiful animation go in a move?
column2: At the finish of the move, never delaying the response to the button press.

column1: When are long wind-up animations acceptable?
column2: When risk and reward balance: the wind-up is the risk, the payoff (huge damage, instant kill) is the reward, like in Mark of Kri.

column1: Character-relative or camera-relative: what is Rogers' core rule?
column2: Pick one for the whole game and stick with it. Never alternate.

column1: What happens to the hero in 'Terror Zombie Death Mansion 3'?
column2: The camera flips 180° between rooms, left now moves him right, and he walks into a zombie who eats his brains.

column1: What is an actuator for?
column2: Vibration (rumble) feedback.

column1: When should rumble fire, per Rogers?
column2: Mainly when the player takes damage or earns a reward, with a consistent language and not all the time.

column1: How did Silent Hill use actuators?
column2: Two actuators at different frequencies simulated a heartbeat when the character was scared or hurt.

column1: What is the key rule for gyroscope controls?
column2: Clearly communicate which way to turn the controller, and remind players the option exists (it's hidden).

column1: Name three games Rogers cites for gyro uses.
column2: Heavenly Sword (nudge arrows), Ratchet & Clank: Tools of Destruction (steer falling characters), Super Mario Galaxy (flip a level).

column1: What makes motion-controlled actions feel less 'floaty' or 'gamey'?
column2: Tuning animation and physics: the right timing, speed and sense of friction.

column1: Lag vs latency?
column2: Lag: delay between an action and seeing it on screen. Latency: online delay in receiving and decoding game data.

column1: Which game let players adjust for lag?
column2: Guitar Hero lets players adjust the lag to match their own skill level.

column1: Why keep motion-control movements broad?
column2: Precise, subtle motions often don't register with motion-sensing cameras.

column1: Motion glyphs should be simple shapes like circles, triangles and ____. Even figure eights and squares get misread.
column2: lines

column1: Motion games that use motion for every action got mocked as ____.
column2: waggle-fests

column1: Apple's minimum touch target is ____ points; Material's is 48×48 dp.
Ergonomics is the study of fitting ____ to the worker.
column2: equipment

column1: Scenario: playtesters tap a locked shop tab and nothing happens. They think the game froze. Which truth?
column2: Use negative responses as well as positive ones. Never let an input do nothing.

column1: Scenario: your hero's sword swing plays a 0.6 s flourish before the hit lands and players feel 'laggy controls'. Fix?
column2: Press = act: the hit starts on the press, and the flourish moves to the end of the move. Or make it a deliberate high-reward wind-up.

column1: Scenario: your new idle game requires 10 taps per second to progress, and reviews mention auto-clickers. Which book lesson?
column2: The pencil trick: don't force players into workarounds. Add automation or hold-to-repeat.

column1: Scenario: in your mobile brawler, the attack button sits top-right and settings sit bottom-right. What principle is broken?
column2: Ergonomics and quick vs slow placement (Fitts's law): frequent quick actions go big and in the thumb zone, rare ones small and far.

column1: Scenario: your match-3 swaps with a pinch gesture instead of swipe or tap. Players struggle. Which truth?
column2: Emulate same-genre control schemes. Familiarity relieves confusion.

column1: Scenario: your game vibrates on every UI tap, match, ad and popup. Players disable haptics. What went wrong?
column2: No consistent haptic language. Reserve vibration for meaningful moments (damage, rewards, big combos).

column1: Scenario: your FTUE unlocks 6 buttons in the first 2 minutes. Which caution applies?
column2: Teach one new move at a time and don't jam features in too quickly (Brütal Legend lesson).

column1: Scenario: a tilt-to-dodge mechanic is never discovered by 70% of players. Fix?
column2: Gyro controls are hidden: clearly show which way to tilt and remind players. Also offer a touch alternative.

column1: Scenario: you want new players' first 10 seconds in your action game to feel amazing before they understand anything. Which book idea?
column2: Make any input (even mashing) produce something cool, like God of War. Auto-attack achieves this on mobile.

column1: Why do fixed top-down cameras avoid the character vs camera-relative problem on mobile?
column2: The camera never rotates, so joystick up always equals screen up and world up.

column1: Why offset a dragged piece above the finger on touchscreens?
column2: The finger hides what it touches. Offsetting keeps the piece and its landing spot visible.

column1: What do MMO and FPS players do with hotkeys and macros, and what should designers offer?
column2: They chain attacks or spell effects (like Combustion, Icy Veins and Fireball) to boost damage per second. Offer customizable controls.

column1: Which Street Fighter II move shows that not everyone can master ultra-complex inputs, and what is Rogers' advice?
column2: The dragon punch. To stay accessible to other player types, don't go nuts with ubercomplex controls.

column1: In Maximo, which buttons map to the overhead swing and the horizontal swing, and why?
column2: Triangle (the top button) = overhead swing, echoing the high-to-low motion. Square (on the horizontal plane of the buttons) = horizontal swing.

column1: What does Brütal Legend do when the hero learns a new move?
column2: It stops the game and shows a full-screen graphic, so the unlock is a big event.

column1: Which keys or buttons usually make a character jump in a platformer?
column2: Space bar, X or A. It is a genre convention players already know.

column1: Name the APTA exercises Rogers lists for gamers' thumb (not the posture tips).
column2: Tap each finger with the same-hand thumb 5 times; alternate palm and back of hand on the thigh 20 times; spread fingers 10 seconds x 8; clasp hands and extend arms forward 10 seconds x 8; fold hands and extend arms overhead 10 seconds x 8.

column1: How does Rogers define camera-relative vs character-relative controls, and which does he prefer?
column2: Camera-relative: controls change with which way the character faces the camera. Character-relative: controls always follow the character, so left is always left even if the camera turns 180 degrees. He prefers character-relative.

column1: What did the Wii Remote and Project Natal open up, and what did Rogers cover first?
column2: A chance to recreate real-world moves as controls. First he showed how to get the most reality out of traditional controllers (e.g., Pitfall's canteen).

column1: What does WarioWare: Smooth Moves show about gyro controls?
column2: You can get away with silliness. Only about 20 moves (half were button presses), but bizarre holds like a mohawk or a spatula flip make players look silly, and that is the fun.

column1: Why build breaks and varied motions into motion-controlled games?
column2: Many players don't play to exercise, so breaks and changing motions prevent wearing out and repetitive stress injuries (unless weight loss is the goal).

column1: What problems can latency cause, and whose job is it mostly?
column2: Lag, control lock-up, sound distortion, freezes or crashes. It is more a programming issue: tightly written code avoids unnecessary data transmission.

column1: What are actuators and gyroscopes in a controller, and what do they enable?
column2: Parts that make most motion controllers (Wii, PS3) possible. Actuator = vibration feedback. Gyroscope = rotating the controller to manipulate on-screen elements.

column1: Why didn't 'everyone on the team holds it that way' prove the creative director right?
column2: The team had been told to hold it that way. Rogers tried the grip and did worse, and later testing proved the QTE too hard.

column1: How does Rogers define the HUD?
column2: Any visual element that communicates information to the player.

column1: What is the HUD named after?
column2: The heads-up display in modern (fighter) aircraft.

column1: List the 7 classic HUD elements.
column2: Health bar/lives, targeting reticule, ammo gauge, inventory, score/experience, radar/map, context-sensitive prompt.

column1: What is the winning formula for any HUD system?
column2: Clear, clean, simple.

column1: Which HUD element does Rogers call the most flexible?
column2: The health bar.

column1: What is a "damage bar"?
column2: An inverted health bar that fills as you take damage; when it is full, the player dies.

column1: How does Star Wars: X-Wing represent health?
column2: As shields. When all shields are gone, the next hit destroys you. Shields can also show as a numeric %.

column1: How does Assassin's Creed use health as a story device?
column2: Stray from the "correct" story and the narrator objects; you are reset to the right point in the story.

column1: Why does Rogers prefer regenerating "wait for health" (Halo) to a game-over screen?
column2: A death/game-over screen pulls the player out of the game; regen keeps them in it.

column1: What is the main danger of screen-effect health (blood smears, red blur)?
column2: Obscuring the view so much that the player cannot see the action.

column1: Your mobile horror game needs a near-death cue that does not cover the screen. Which book ideas fit?
column2: A haptic heartbeat (Silent Hill rumble), heartbeat and breathing audio, and light edge darkening (Call of Duty, Uncharted 2), without obscuring the view.

column1: Why can white reticules be a problem?
column2: They become hard to see on some surfaces and backgrounds.

column1: Why should a reticule change color or sharpen over a target?
column2: It cues the player when to fire.

column1: Reticule "stickiness" is also known as ____.
column2: aim assist

column1: How does Team Fortress 2 build gameplay into its sniper reticule?
column2: The zoomed reticule projects a laser dot that enemies can see and try to dodge.

column1: Why must ammo gauges be especially visible in games like Resident Evil 2?
column2: Ammo is scarce, so it is one of the most-watched readouts.

column1: Why display ammo even for an infinite-ammo weapon (Metal Slug)?
column2: It still tells the player which weapon is armed.

column1: How should players access multiple ammo types (Ratchet & Clank)?
column2: Bring them up with a button press.

column1: What two input methods give quick inventory access?
column2: Hotkeys and drag-and-drop.

column1: How does Diablo turn inventory into a puzzle?
column2: Each item has a size in a limited grid; players try to fit as much as possible.

column1: What progression does Rogers suggest for restricted inventories?
column2: Let it expand: pouch, then backpack, then a magic bag of infinite holding.

column1: What is Resident Evil 2's "magic box"?
column2: Items stored in one box appear in boxes found later, so there is no backtracking.

column1: Inventory items, realistic or iconic, need clear ____ and simple color schemes.
column2: silhouettes

column1: Which game replaced score bars with text combo meters (2001)?
column2: Devil May Cry.

column1: What brought scoring back after stat tracking replaced high scores?
column2: Online leaderboards.

column1: Why does Rogers say you cannot overdo congratulating the player?
column2: Games easily make players feel clumsy but rarely make them feel brilliant, so praise needs to be loud.

column1: Which game showers success with fireworks and back-flipping pirate rabbits?
column2: Zack & Wiki: Quest for Barbaros' Treasure.

column1: Give the 6 reward pointers.
column2: Voice/SFX; freeze or hero celebrates; tons of particles; clear cause and effect (coin flies to tally); readable font, mind text length; fill the screen but never cover gameplay.

column1: What is the "cause and effect" example for scoring?
column2: A collected coin travels up to the tally with a Las Vegas-style cha-ching.

column1: The first game radar/map appeared in ____ (Namco, 1980).
column2: Rally-X

column1: Why should players be able to read the map while moving?
column2: Opening a map, memorizing it and closing it is a chore that breaks the flow of play.

column1: What does GTA4 let players do with the map?
column2: Place their own markers, which then guide them to the objective.

column1: Why must maps indicate elevation, and how?
column2: Multi-level spaces confuse players easily; use a color code or onion-skin effect to show the current layer.

column1: Why should you never re-fog cleared areas of a fog-of-war map?
column2: It confuses players with the very tool meant to help them navigate.

column1: Name the three extra map aids Rogers cites.
column2: Distance-to-goal counter (Batman: AA), guard detection cones (Metal Gear), NPC names on the map (Harry Potter: Order of the Phoenix).

column1: What is a context-sensitive prompt?
column2: A small icon or line of text that shows up when the player stands near something usable, usually displaying the button to press.

column1: What were Maximo's "plings"?
column2: Emoticon prompts that showed when the player could NOT do an action as well as when they could.

column1: How can plings make NPC interactions deeper?
column2: They show the NPC's mood; a good mood gives a better response or reward than angry, scared or sad.

column1: First step to a clean screen?
column2: Fade or move inactive HUD off screen, bring it back when relevant, and offer a quick button to call it up.

column1: Which game conveyed almost everything without HUD through sound, animation and VFX?
column2: Peter Jackson's King Kong (Ubisoft, 2005).

column1: What is the Scooby-Doo effect?
column2: Flat-colored interactive objects stand out against detailed painted backgrounds (Hanna-Barbera); use it deliberately.

column1: Name the two "planets" of interface.
column2: Planet No Interface and Planet Gobs of Interface (RPGs, RTSs, sims, adventure, some shooters).

column1: KYSS = Keep Your ____ ____.
column2: Symbols Simple

column1: What does the postage-stamp anecdote teach?
column2: Icon images must be current: younger testers did not recognize a postage stamp used for an ink-stamp function.

column1: Why avoid text in icons? (2 reasons)
column2: It must be redone for localization, and it may be too small to read.

column1: When color is not enough to tell icons apart, use ____.
column2: shape

column1: What outline does Rogers recommend for icons?
column2: A strong black or white outline so they pop off the background.

column1: How often should a unit's voice confirmation play on clicks?
column2: Sparingly: rotate several recorded variants so the same line never returns sooner than about three clicks later.

column1: Which buttons should be the biggest?
column2: The most important one, and the most-used one.

column1: What inspired Maximo's ability icons?
column2: Boy Scout merit badges.

column1: Why should programmers not design icons alone?
column2: They care about function, not design or art.

column1: Classic icon meanings: skull? coin? exclamation point over the hero?
column2: Danger/poison/death; money; the hero can interact with something.

column1: Define a QTE.
column2: A prompt forcing a split-second action, or you suffer (usually painful or fatal) consequences.

column1: Which game introduced QTEs, and which named and revived them?
column2: Dragon's Lair (1983) introduced them; Shenmue (1999) revived and named them.

column1: Rogers' QTE timing rule?
column2: One beat to process the icon, another beat to press the button.

column1: Why does Rogers dislike random QTE prompts?
column2: They make players feel they won by luck, not skill; predictability lets them enjoy the action.

column1: Why should QTEs avoid shoulder buttons?
column2: They are harder to reach; QTEs should stick to one easy control set (face buttons or a stick).

column1: Where should HUD never go (with exceptions)?
column2: The center of the screen, except reticules, targeting or labels identifying game objects.

column1: Why place the most important info top-left?
column2: Western eyes read left to right, so the eye flows back into the game on the right.

column1: What is the bracketing effect?
column2: HUD on the left, right and bottom edges makes the screen feel small and claustrophobic, like a mail slot.

column1: Why does Dead Space let enemies attack while you browse inventory?
column2: To deny the "gamey" world-freeze and build dread.

column1: You should never have to press a button more than ____ times to reach any game screen.
column2: three

column1: Rogers' button-press war story: from ____ presses to gameplay down to ____.
Name the 4 title-screen styles.
column2: Movie poster, heroic pose, enigmatic image, logo screen.

column1: Your pause menu lists Resume, Options, Help, then Save, and players save constantly. Fix it the Rogers way.
column2: Let the pause button close the menu (drop Resume) and put Save, the most common choice, first.

column1: How many save files does Rogers recommend at minimum, and why?
column2: At least three: replays, backups against catastrophic choices, other players.

column1: What is a save "reset system", and why avoid it?
column2: Reloading is easier than dying and restarting, so saving becomes a gameplay mechanic; it breaks immersion.

column1: Why must loading screens show a moving image and a progress indicator?
column2: Motion shows the game has not crashed (hardware makers require it); a progress bar or % shows how long to wait.

column1: Your loading screen shows the same control tip every time. Which rule is broken?
column2: Do not repeat tips; never show control tips the player has already seen.

column1: What three qualities must legal screens have?
column2: Legible, accurate and skippable.

column1: Which games have fun credits?
column2: LittleBigPlanet (entertaining sequence) and Typing of the Dead (type the credits).

column1: What does "gestalt" mean in games?
column2: German for "whole": the overall feel of an experience.

column1: Why never place red text on black?
column2: It blurs on many TVs (old sets, composite cables) and has low contrast.

column1: Rogers found any font under ____ point very hard to read on standard-definition TVs.
Which game's tiny text made objectives unreadable on SD TVs?
column2: Dead Rising (2006).

column1: Your mobile shooter's fire button sits under the notch in one landscape orientation. Which principle?
column2: Safe area / safe frame: keep HUD away from clipped edges and inside the guaranteed-visible area.

column1: Players say your 4X lobby feels "cramped" with icons on every edge. Which effect?
column2: The bracketing effect (mail-slot screen). Consolidate into hubs and collapse rails.

column1: New players can't find the PLAY button among 14 icons. Which icon rule fixes it?
column2: The most important (and most-used) button must be the biggest.

column1: Reaching your event shop takes 5 taps from the lobby. Which rule is broken?
column2: The Three-Press (Three-Tap) Rule.

column1: Rarity tiers differ only by red vs green frames. What is the risk?
column2: Red-green color-blind players cannot tell them apart. Add shape or pattern coding (color is not enough).

column1: Your boss finisher QTE uses random prompts and players call it unfair. What do you change?
column2: Make it predictable (same pattern), give a beat to see and a beat to press, and consider making it optional.

column1: Players can't tell how they earned coins after a level. What should you add?
column2: Clear cause and effect: coins fly from the action into the counter with a sound.

column1: Your German build overflows every button. Which two Rogers warnings apply?
column2: Watch text length, and avoid text in icons (localization). Budget about 30% expansion.

column1: Players lose a life when a phone call interrupts a level. What should happen?
column2: Auto-pause and save state on app backgrounding, then resume gracefully.

column1: Your home screen shows red dots that never clear. Why is this harmful?
column2: Players learn to ignore all dots, so the signal dies (it is also a dark pattern).

column1: Your sword-combat icons and fire-spell icons are both plain red. What does Rogers advise?
column2: Color-code by category but use a different shade of red for each, and add shape differences.

column1: A new stamp tool uses a postage-stamp icon and teen testers are confused. Which rule?
column2: Use current, accurate images, because metaphors age.

column1: Your tutorial hand pointer never goes away and veterans complain. Which principle?
column2: The clean screen: fade HUD elements when they are not needed and bring them back only when relevant.

column1: How does the book's worked example of voice acknowledgments on icon clicks clarify the "every third click" rule?
column2: It cycles three different lines (click 1, 2, 3) and only returns to the first on click 4, so the same line never repeats sooner than about three clicks; record extra cues to avoid repetition.

column1: What two kinds of rating can a tally screen show, and what are the book's word-rating examples?
column2: A letter grade (A, B, C) or a word rating, such as "Awesome Dude" or "Master of the Universe".

column1: Name six things a level-end tally screen can count.
column2: Any six of: score, completion time, shooting accuracy, enemies slain, money remaining/collected/spent, lives, a rating, objectives completed, secrets found as X/Y, or silly stats like blood spilled, distance travelled and chests smashed.

column1: What are Rogers' four meanings of 'level'?
column2: A place where play happens; a slice of space for one gameplay experience; a progress counter; a player/character rank.

column1: Where does the game term 'level' most likely come from?
column2: Dungeons & Dragons: players descended dungeon levels (like floors) to reach the dragon.

column1: How does Rogers define a 'world'?
column2: A location defined mainly by its visual or genre theme, which may contain several locations sharing that theme.

column1: What does 'wave' mean as a level term?
column2: Combat repetition: enemy after enemy while you keep doing the same thing (e.g. Plants vs. Zombies).

column1: What does 'stage' usually emphasize, and where is it common?
column2: Clear separations between activities (like rocket stages); common for boss phases.

column1: Super Mario Bros.' World 1-1 should really be called ____.
column2: Level 1-1

column1: Why did 'worlds' end up containing several 'levels'?
column2: Home games needed longer play, so devs reused one texture set and mechanics across several levels inside one themed world.

column1: Name the top 10 cliché level themes.
column2: Outer space, fire/ice, dungeon/cavern/tomb, factory, jungle, spooky/haunted/graveyard, pirate, gritty urban, space station, sewer.

column1: Why did fire/ice levels become so popular?
column2: Easy-to-code hazards (flames, slippery floors) that break rhythm, ready-made themed enemies, and red/blue color that made screenshots stand out.

column1: Why did outer space suit the earliest games?
column2: A black screen already looked like space, ships needed no animation and could be simple shapes, and gameplay could be pure physics, before games had artists or designers.

column1: What is Rogers' recipe for a good scare?
column2: Pace it: quiet, then a distraction, then the scare. The best scare is expected but its source is unknown.

column1: Which cliché theme does Rogers call the most adaptable?
column2: Spooky/haunted (it's been used in adventures, platformers, RPGs, FPSs and puzzle games).

column1: The gritty urban theme lets players ____ a world like the one outside their door.
column2: improve or destroy

column1: What is the Mexican pizza technique?
column2: Combine two things that don't seem to belong together to create something surprisingly good and original.

column1: Your LiveOps team only has pirate and winter assets left but needs a fresh event theme. Which technique?
column2: Mexican pizza: combine them, e.g. a frozen pirate-ship event (like Maximo's ice-covered pirate level).

column1: What are Rogers' five file-naming tips?
column2: About 8 characters max; no wit, just location + order; systematic abbreviations (fac01s01); never one abbreviation for two meanings; organized folders with shared/tracked files.

column1: What are the four schools of player-facing level names?
column2: Functional (numbers), location, descriptive, punny.

column1: Why are functional (numbered) level names weak, per Rogers?
column2: Players don't know the highest number, so they can't judge overall progress, and numbers lack personality.

column1: Why should descriptive level names be used with care?
column2: They can tip your hand and spoil surprises in the plot or level.

column1: You plan a punny event name for a game launching in 15 languages. What's the risk?
column2: Puns rarely survive localization; keep important names translatable.

column1: Disneyland's hierarchy: world → land → attraction → ____.
column2: scene

column1: Video game hierarchy: world → level → experience → ____.
column2: moment-to-moment gameplay

column1: What are Disneyland's five original lands, and which of Walt's passions inspired each?
column2: Frontierland (history), Tomorrowland (progress), Adventureland (nature), Fantasyland (his animated films), Main Street (childhood hometown).

column1: Your producer wants a lavish illustrated world map before production starts. What does the team actually need?
column2: A simple flowchart showing where the player goes, what they find there, and the order/spatial relationships.

column1: What did Donkey Kong's 'how high can you get?' screen teach?
column2: Showing how many stages remain sets a goal and whets the player's appetite.

column1: What mapping advance did Ghosts 'n Goblins make?
column2: A 'you are here' icon followed by a camera pan over the whole world, teasing what's to come.

column1: Why does Mortal Kombat's mostly-locked character grid work as a map?
column2: It shows progression without physical travel, foreshadows future opponents, and drives the urge to unlock them all.

column1: Why is a scare bigger when the player knows it's coming?
column2: The waiting builds anticipation, which matters as much as the delivery.

column1: You want players to anticipate a feature that unlocks at level 50. Which Disneyland/BioShock trick can you use from level 1?
column2: Posters: show teasers or locked icons early that only pay off once the feature unlocks.

column1: What are the four player goals drawn from Disneyland's stories?
column2: Escape/survive, explore, educate, moral.

column1: Which storytelling tools go with explore and with educate?
column2: Explore: freedom of mobility and conversation. Educate: observation and imitation.

column1: How should a level deliver a moral goal?
column2: Through choice and consequence, with the choices affecting gameplay.

column1: A level exists only to teach driving. Which designer question did that answer?
column2: 'What is the player's objective in this level?'

column1: What are the 11 minimum rows of a beat chart?
column2: Level name, file name, player's objective, story beat, play style, enemies, mechanics, NPCs, bonus materials, time of day, color mapping.

column1: What does a beat chart reveal?
column2: Gaps and clumping (and repetition) across the whole game, so you can spread elements out.

column1: Why build a beat chart before building assets?
column2: A few hours of spotting patterns improves production, gameplay and art before anything costly is built.

column1: Your beat chart shows three night levels in a row. Fix?
column2: Vary time of day and weather (morning, evening, rain, snow).

column1: Your match-3 sheet shows the coolest blocker first appears at level 200. Which Relic Raider lesson applies?
column2: Late introduction (like the late driving levels): bring it in earlier.

column1: What is the rule of three for gameplay systems?
column2: If a system is used fewer than three times in the game, it isn't worth having.

column1: Why can't the car system also run a motorcycle or hovercraft?
column2: They behave too differently. Reuse has limits even within ground vehicles.

column1: Your team proposes a co-op boss raid that 'just reuses' the collect-items event framework. Which lesson applies?
column2: The vehicle-system limit (the hovercraft): a feature that behaves differently needs a different system.

column1: Unless it's a driving game, never follow a driving level with ____.
column2: more driving

column1: Which developer does Rogers praise for milking a small palette of mechanics?
column2: Treasure (Gunstar Heroes, Dynamite Headdy, Ikaruga).

column1: What's the difference between an alley and an island level?
column2: Alley: a directed path to a goal. Island: an open space players experience in any order.

column1: Name the seven advantages of alley levels.
column2: Easy camera triggers, dramatic camera moves, optional removal of camera controls, scripted events, choreographed combat/traps, bottlenecks against backtracking, illusional narrative.

column1: Why are island levels harder to design?
column2: The camera must handle all widths and heights, scripted events can be missed, fights can be skipped, and façades fail because everything is seen from every side.

column1: What are the four advantages of island levels?
column2: Sense of space and scale; exploration with secrets in in-between spaces; a smorgasbord of options; vehicles feel better. Also great for multiplayer.

column1: What is a weenie?
column2: A landmark that grabs attention and draws players toward it (castle, mountain, statue, bridge, tree, rock).

column1: Where does the term 'weenie' come from?
column2: Walt Disney named it after the hot dog that animal trainers waved to lure dog actors across a set.

column1: Playtesters exit a side area behind a house and walk back the way they came. Rogers' fix?
column2: Place a landmark (weenie) at the exit so they can re-orient.

column1: Why should even sandbox games prompt players toward the next thing?
column2: A world where you can do anything at any time is intimidating and confusing, whatever players claim.

column1: Why does Crackdown give each city zone its own theme?
column2: To aid navigation and orientation (like Disneyland's lands) and to match each zone to the gang that runs it.

column1: On a top-down graph-paper map, what is the usual scale?
column2: The player equals one square; everything else is drawn relative to that.

column1: What belongs in a level-map legend?
column2: Player start, enemy starts, doors/teleporters/gates, puzzle mechanics, chests/power-ups, traps with area of effect, significant landmarks.

column1: Why should top-down map passages be five squares wide?
column2: Player plus two widths each side leaves room to navigate, fight and move the camera; first designs are usually too cramped.

column1: What is the squint test?
column2: Squint until your eyes are nearly closed; the brightest thing on screen should be the main path (Naughty Dog's trick).

column1: Your home screen's shop banner is brighter than the Play button. Which test does it fail?
column2: The squint test: the main action should be the brightest thing.

column1: While describing a level you say 'then the player walks over to the bridge'. What does Rogers say to do?
column2: Cut that section. Walking is never gameplay.

column1: List the ten alternatives to walking.
column2: Jumping, fighting, collecting, climbing, swimming, swinging, flying, escaping, sneaking, exploring.

column1: Rogers' backtracking motto: show the player the ____ first, then let them find the key.
column2: door

column1: Players must return to the same courtyard for the third time. What should you change?
column2: The location itself: add new combat or collectibles, or alter the terrain (e.g. an earthquake creates jumpable hills).

column1: If it ever feels long or boring, then ____.
column2: it is

column1: What is a finger in level design?
column2: A short dead-end branch off the main path that makes a linear level feel explorable.

column1: What must every finger have?
column2: A reward at its end, even if it's just a trash can.

column1: Why add fingers instead of full alternate paths?
column2: They make a level feel deeper and explored without building complex geometry or paths players may never take.

column1: A tappable chest on your saga map does nothing when tapped. Which rule does it break?
column2: Every finger needs a reward: optional exploration must always pay off.

column1: How do you show elevations on a top-down map without clutter?
column2: Layer them on tracing paper or a light board, split by player height, clearly labeled in order.

column1: Besides the legend, what else should go on level maps?
column2: Spawn points with aggro radius, bread-crumb collectibles, secret entrances/breakable walls, obstacles and barriers, special terrain (cursed earth, swamp, ice, lava).

column1: What is illusional narrative?
column2: Showing two or more scenes (before/after) so players fill in the event between them, like a comic-book gutter or a film cut.

column1: Why use illusional narrative?
column2: Big production savings: real-time animated events are slow to make and must be redone when the level changes.

column1: How do you keep illusional narrative in story order?
column2: Gating: bottlenecks, camera views, checkpoints, toggling elements on/off, or doors.

column1: What is a gray box level?
column2: An untextured blockout built in an art tool that shows scale, size and relationships against camera and character metrics.

column1: A gray-box pace-out of a 30-minute level should take about ____.
column2: 15 minutes

column1: Rogers suggests changing the player's emotion every ____ minutes.
Which five emotions does Rogers say most games deliver?
column2: Aggression, fear, surprise, joy, disappointment.

column1: Your event runs three boss fights back to back and players report fatigue. Which principle?
column2: Big vs small moments: don't stack big moments; add quiet breathers.

column1: Why must weather affect every element of a level?
column2: If even one element ignores it, the whole effect breaks.

column1: How do big and tight spaces feel, and what combat suits each?
column2: Big spaces feel safe and suit large enemy groups; tight spaces feel mysterious/dangerous and suit one-on-one fights.

column1: What is Rogers' golden rule of level design?
column2: If it looks like the player can go there, they should be able to.

column1: Players tap a grayed-out icon and nothing happens, with no explanation. Which rule is violated?
column2: The golden rule / no invisible walls: if it looks interactive it should respond, so explain why it's locked.

column1: Why does right-to-left movement make Western players uneasy?
column2: They're used to reading and viewing information left to right.

column1: What is a sphincter twitcher?
column2: A thin platform over great danger (heights, lava, whirlpools), ideally under a bird's-eye camera; it feels deadly even if it's safe.

column1: What's the lesson of the architecturally accurate buildings story?
column2: Don't be bound by realism: omit anything that doesn't serve gameplay or story (like the Death Star's unseen toilets).

column1: What is a playground, and what do you test there?
column2: A non-shipping gray box for mechanics and hazards: ground angles (walk/run/IK), boxes at many heights (jump, hoist, teeter, double/wall jumps), hazard distance/timing/lethality.

column1: What is a combat arena?
column2: A test space for combat systems, cover systems and enemies, with quick spawning of enemy combinations.

column1: Why do training levels usually end up neglected?
column2: They get left to the end (key lessons not known yet, best art comes late, players will learn along the way), then schedules crunch.

column1: Your team will build the FTUE in the final two weeks 'when art is final'. What would Rogers advise?
column2: Build it first (rough art is fine) before designer blinders set in, or better, make the whole game teach progressively.

column1: What are B.H. Liddell Hart's three elements of combat?
column2: Guarding, hitting and moving.

column1: Why does violence give games the quickest positive feedback loop?
column2: It's graphic and visceral: the player acts, instantly sees a result (the enemy dies) and gets a reward. Freud's pleasure principle: ring the bell, get the treat.

column1: Name the five ESRB violence-related descriptors Rogers lists.
column2: Comic mischief, cartoon violence, fantasy violence, violence, intense violence.

column1: Violence is all about ____: it feels more violent when the player does it.
column2: context

column1: List the areas Rogers' rating self-check questions cover.
column2: Whether the player commits it (realistic weapons?), how often, whether it's rewarded or shown as inappropriate, how graphic (dismemberment, lingering camera), residue (blood, gibs), and whether it targets bad guys who suffer.

column1: Why are romance, comedy and conversation rarely gameplay, per Rogers?
column2: They're hard to recreate, so teams explore them less, players keep buying familiar genres, and publishers find new styles harder to sell.

column1: What should decide a character's combat moves first?
column2: Their personality, then the genre and desired experience, which point to their weapons.

column1: The four ranges of combat: close, medium, long and ____.
column2: area effect

column1: Name the four attack elevations.
column2: Standing, low, high, aerial.

column1: How is a high attack delivered, and what is it for?
column2: Jump, then attack. Used against flying or large enemies like bosses.

column1: Why should each elevation you use get its own attack set?
column2: Each elevation makes the player handle combat in a different way.

column1: An enemy wears a helmet that deflects overhead strikes. Following Maximo, how do you beat it?
column2: Use a horizontal attack, the opposite direction.

column1: What seven columns belong in an attack matrix?
column2: Attack name, control scheme, range, speed, direction, damage (label plus number or %), special.

column1: In Rogers' sample matrix, what makes the Jump strike special?
column2: Slow and downward, strong (25 hp), and it stuns any target within a two-unit radius.

column1: What frame rate should you aim for in combat?
column2: 60 fps. 30 can work, but lag and stutter hurt combat.

column1: Why avoid long wind-up animations on normal attacks?
column2: They throw off the player's timing, so they miss or strike when they don't mean to.

column1: What is a lunge?
column2: A fluid thrust that returns the character to their original standing position.

column1: What's the typical input window for continuing a combat chain?
column2: Usually within about a second.

column1: Why must chained attacks move the character forward?
column2: Knocked-back enemies would drift out of reach, so later hits in the chain would miss.

column1: Your hero wields a giant two-handed axe. Is a long wind-up OK?
column2: Yes. Heavy or oversized weapons justify long wind-ups as risk vs. reward.

column1: Give the VFX examples Rogers cites for attacks.
column2: Slice streaks and speed lines (Onimusha), fire trails and blood splatter (MadWorld), and screen-filling debris, dust and lightning on big moves.

column1: Your memory budget can't fit enemy reaction animations. What's the minimum fix?
column2: Hit effects and sound effects (ideally a vocal reaction) that confirm the hit landed.

column1: Name three ways to hype a powerful strike.
column2: Camera shake, controller rumble, slow motion.

column1: Close battles are more ____.
column2: exciting

column1: People want to play games that make them ____.
column2: look cool

column1: When are QTEs usually triggered in combat?
column2: When an enemy or boss reaches a certain health level.

column1: List Rogers' five QTE tips.
column2: Reserve them for bombastic attacks; same prompt location; allow a beat to react; return quickly after a failure; substantial damage instead of instant death.

column1: Reaching a QTE took three attack patterns and the player failed it. What should they redo?
column2: Just one pattern before the QTE triggers again.

column1: What did The Mark of Kri's targeting system introduce?
column2: A radar-style analog-stick sweep to queue up a sequence of enemies. It was patented.

column1: Why should weapon upgrades show visually on the weapon?
column2: A '+3' stat bump gives players neither the gameplay information nor the visual reward they deserve.

column1: How should weapons react to stone or metal vs wood?
column2: Rebound off stone and metal; blades sink into wood.

column1: Giant-axe hero, arena full of unbreakable stone pillars. What happens, and why design it this way?
column2: The axe rebounds off the pillars and gives enemies openings. It uses world collision to create an arena-specific challenge.

column1: Why must stealth kills only work under specific conditions?
column2: Otherwise players spam them instead of regular attacks, which makes them an exploit and the move goes stale.

column1: Why are grapples technically hard to build?
column2: Two-character collision: both characters must animate together to look natural and avoid clipping (sorting).

column1: What four lock-on HUD markers does the book show?
column2: Floor marker, pointer arrow, glowing aura, health bar over the target.

column1: How does the later Zelda lock-on handle switching and kills?
column2: Hold to lock, flick the stick to switch left or right, and it auto-latches onto the next enemy after a kill.

column1: A player keeps missing and dying. What two fixes does 'Now You Have to Kiss Me' suggest?
column2: Dynamically enlarge enemy collision, or offer to lower the difficulty.

column1: What is 'the graveyard hustle'?
column2: WoW slang for dying and running back from the graveyard. It's what happens when a dodge doesn't fully clear an attack.

column1: Why add a recovery beat after a dodge?
column2: It lets players reorient and stops them using dodges as a movement exploit.

column1: During a roll, the camera keeps hitting the hazard. What's Rogers' fix?
column2: Lock the camera in place during the dodge, then let it catch up once the player is clear.

column1: Your brawler's dash only moves them. What would Rogers add?
column2: Make it do something too: ram enemies, smash breakables, hit several foes, or knock enemies flying.

column1: What is a recoil bounce?
column2: After a jump attack hits, the player bounces a short distance away so they don't land on or next to the enemy.

column1: A jump-attack hitbox should be like a good pair of pants: plenty of room in the ____.
column2: seat (butt)

column1: What's the rule for jump height vs enemy height?
column2: The max jump must be taller than the tallest enemy you can jump-attack.

column1: Your gritty soldier looks silly jumping. What's the alternative?
column2: Vaulting over obstacles. It pairs with cover and ducking (Gears of War 2 shows a prompt).

column1: General vs positional blocks?
column2: General: one button, all-purpose (action games). Positional: tied to high or low height (fighting games).

column1: How should a successful block be confirmed?
column2: A loud CLANG sound effect or sparks, never blood.

column1: Two ways to stop players camping behind a block?
column2: Breakable shields, or enemy knockback (block-breaking) attacks.

column1: Why did Maximo 2 make the shield unbreakable?
column2: In Maximo 1, players treated the breakable shield as a limited resource and avoided using it. Unbreakable, they happily blocked.

column1: F2P players hoard your limited revive tokens and never use them. Which Rogers lesson applies?
column2: Maximo's breakable shield: limited resources get hoarded. Make them more plentiful, regenerating, or free and unbreakable.

column1: Name four alternate uses for a shield from the book.
column2: Any four: dash to clear obstacles, smash enemies, throw it, sled down slopes, overhead cover from debris or lava, crowbar, back protection (plus Rygar's chain weapon).

column1: What is encumbrance, and which games suit it?
column2: More armor makes you slower and noisier. It fits RPGs; usually skip it in action games.

column1: What are the six paper doll armor slots?
column2: Head, torso, arms, hands, legs, feet.

column1: Give two examples of armor doubling as a health display.
column2: Dead Space's spine health meter; Ghosts 'N Goblins armor popping off.

column1: What did Mario's Tanooki suit add besides protection?
column2: Flight and the ability to turn into an invincible statue.

column1: Why is armor customization so powerful, per the WoW example?
column2: It customizes without changing the base model, and other players see your gear and want it, so everyone plays longer.

column1: The Three As of ranged combat: Action, ____, Ammo.
column2: Aiming

column1: Which designer said ranged combat is about building a distinctive rhythm?
column2: Hardy LeBel (Halo: Combat Evolved, SOCOM 3).

column1: Your melee adventure hands out a gun in level 1. What does Rogers advise?
column2: Save guns for later. Let players master their moves and attacks first.

column1: How does Gears of War's active reload create risk/reward?
column2: A well-timed manual reload is faster; a botched one is slower and leaves you defenseless longer.

column1: Name four things a reticule may need to communicate.
column2: Any four: aim, bullet spread, recoil, jamming, overheating, ammo, hits vs near misses, friend or foe.

column1: Why play gunshot and impact sounds at full volume regardless of distance?
column2: So players can tell whether their shot landed.

column1: Long open corridors plus high lethality. How will players play?
column2: Cautiously.

column1: Lots of cover, broken sightlines and regenerating health. What rhythm results?
column2: Swirling dogfights: engage, disengage to heal, re-engage.

column1: LeBel: resist making ranged weapons weak, and be ____ to the player.
column2: generous

column1: Per Rogers, how many rounds does a pistol magazine usually hold?
column2: 6 to 15 rounds.

column1: What's the sniper rifle's built-in weakness?
column2: You usually can't fire from the hip, and scope tunnel vision leaves you vulnerable to flankers.

column1: Shotguns and flamethrowers fire in a ____ rather than a straight line.
column2: cone

column1: What are the TF2 Heavy minigun's trade-offs?
column2: It takes time to spin up. You can keep it spinning, but enemies hear you coming.

column1: In the book's weapon matrix, which weapon is 'very strong' at medium range?
column2: The assault rifle.

column1: Why keep weapon overlap minimal?
column2: Distinct weapons make the game feel well rounded, and any overlap should come with a disadvantage.

column1: What is Rogers' friendly fire rule?
column2: It depends on the mode (more logical in PvP than co-op), and players should be able to toggle it.

column1: Why always give a shooter a melee fallback?
column2: Players feel powerless with nothing to shoot. Bashing the baddie keeps things fair and realistic.

column1: What loadout limit and switching rule does Rogers suggest?
column2: A main gun plus a sidearm, switched quickly, ideally with one button.

column1: What's the main pitfall of cover systems?
column2: Being too sticky, so players snap into cover when they don't want to.

column1: List the seven elements of a shooting gallery screen.
column2: Turret, reward object, ground target, edge-justifying scenery, aerial target with hit feedback, smaller aerial target (more points), smaller ground target (more points).

column1: Aerial targets whip past and players fire blindly. What's the fix?
column2: Slow down the targets or the craft, naturally or artificially, so players can line up shots.

column1: What is a rail shooter's unique advantage?
column2: The developer controls the camera and the sequence of events: guaranteed scares, furious shooting, scripted drama.

column1: What are the two smart bomb activation styles?
column2: Instant (Defender) or charge-up (R-Type).

column1: Why ration smart bombs?
column2: If they charge too fast or can be used too often, they wipe out your carefully designed encounters.

column1: What three parts does the book's grenade aim aid have?
column2: A cook meter, an arc range-finder and a target marker.

column1: Fire takes no ____: players get hurt if they wander into it.
column2: sides

column1: Why make antidotes more common than poison?
column2: Never make death feel inevitable. Always give the player a fighting chance.

column1: Name the seven control-loss states.
column2: Stun, knockback, knockdown, latching on, transformation, loss of balance, sliding.

column1: What is 'double bolting'?
column2: From Ratchet & Clank: knocked into another hazard while stunned, you lose double the bolts (currency) before you can collect any.

column1: Your gacha PvP lets players chain 4-second stuns and people rage-quit. Which principle?
column2: Always enable the player, even when disabling them. Add CC immunity windows or diminishing returns.

column1: Using Rogers' formula: the player should survive 25 hits at 8 damage each. Starting health?
What's the health bar's weakness, and the fix?
column2: Small amounts of damage are hard to see. Segment the bar.

column1: Which game pioneered regenerating health in FPS games?
column2: Halo: Combat Evolved.

column1: Why did arcade games have lives?
column2: To keep players feeding in quarters. Extra lives were a short-term goal that kept them going.

column1: What exploit did Doom players use to avoid death?
column2: Reloading a saved file instead of restarting from a checkpoint, so they stopped fearing death.

column1: The player dies in a boss's final phase. What's Rogers' approach?
column2: Let them continue the fight as if nothing happened, or restore only a little boss health. Never a full replay.

column1: Your match-3 fail screen plays 6 seconds of sad animation before Retry appears. Which rule is broken?
column2: Kill quickly and make the path back to gameplay as fast as possible.

column1: On failure, players lose the run's loot AND their streak AND a life. Which rule is broken?
column2: Don't double-punish (the F2P version of double bolting).

column1: Rogers' Very Important Thing about death: you want to ____.
column2: keep them playing

column1: What is Rogers' 'keep going' screen?
column2: A replacement for game over that previews the next level, story beat, treasure, weapon or power-up, to excite the player into continuing.

column1: What is Rogers' golden rule of enemy design?
column2: Form follows function: define what the enemy does before how it looks.

column1: Why must enemy function be decided before its look?
column2: Coding, rigging/animation and texturing all depend on it; redoing enemies kills morale and wastes time and money.

column1: Name the seven enemy attributes.
column2: Size, behavior, speed, movement, attacks, aggression, health.

column1: Why does aggression get its own line even though it's part of behavior?
column2: Combat is often treated by designers as its own system.

column1: What are the five enemy size classes?
column2: Short, average, large, huge, gigantic.

column1: A 'huge' enemy is at least ____ the player's size.
column2: twice

column1: What defines a 'gigantic' enemy?
column2: It's so large it can only be completely seen from a distance.

column1: How many 'heads' tall is an average human vs a heroic character?
column2: About 7 heads vs about 8.5 heads.

column1: What does 'fight your way up' the enemy mean?
column2: Bigger enemies require a wider range of attacks: average = low + medium; huge = low, medium and high.

column1: Players say stomping your tiny cute critters makes them feel mean. Which size principle explains it?
column2: Size affects emotion: beating short enemies can feel like bullying; beating huge ones feels heroic.

column1: What three questions define enemy behavior?
column2: How does it move? What does it do in combat? What does it do when hurt?

column1: What is a patroller?
column2: An enemy moving back and forth or up and down mechanically; always predictable.

column1: What commonly turns a patroller into a chaser?
column2: Spotting the player or being attacked.

column1: Why does a shooter keep its distance?
column2: Its projectile attack works best at range, so it avoids engaging up close.

column1: What is a guard's AI priority?
column2: Protecting an item or location (like a doorway) rather than pursuing the player.

column1: Why are bombers common in 2D games?
column2: 3D cameras make it hard to see enemies directly above the player.

column1: How does a teleporter differ from a burrower?
column2: Teleporting is instant (no window to attack during the move); a burrower has a visible invulnerable repositioning state you wait out.

column1: Players can't ever hit your instant-teleporting enemy. What does Rogers recommend?
column2: Give the player a way to disrupt the teleport, such as a stun or other disruptive attack.

column1: Name four ways to beat a blocker.
column2: Attack from another direction/elevation, disarm it with a specific move, break the shield, or wait out its invulnerability.

column1: What does a doppelganger force the player to do?
column2: Use their own moves or weapons in unusual ways to defeat a copy of themselves.

column1: What is threat analysis?
column2: The player deciding which enemy is the bigger threat, killing it first and defending against the rest.

column1: Why pair a big chaser with small flyers?
column2: Attack the big one and the flyers sting you; chase the flyers and the big one thumps you: a forced priority puzzle.

column1: The five enemy speeds are non-mobile, slow, medium, ____ and quick.
column2: fast

column1: What separates a hazard from an enemy?
column2: Mobility and AI (with exceptions like non-mobile enemies that still have AI).

column1: The Three Ss — speed, size and strength — are ____ proportional.
column2: inversely

column1: Why does a medium enemy that's both strong and fast feel bad?
column2: It has an advantage the player can't match, so it feels cheap, like fighting a computer.

column1: A single slow zombie in your level isn't scary at all. How do you fix it?
column2: Use slow enemies in numbers (a dozen is scary), give them a big hit or a fast attack.

column1: Which Resident Evil enemies show slow movement making a villain feel powerful?
column2: Tyrant, Nemesis and Dr. Salvador.

column1: Why should medium-speed chasers run slightly slower than the player?
column2: So the player can retreat, reorient and face them in time to attack or defend.

column1: Your burst-dashing 'quick' enemy feels unfair. Two fixes?
column2: Limit its attacks and moves, and play a warning animation before each burst.

column1: What did Crash Bandicoot 2 focus groups prefer?
column2: Simple learnable patterns over more behavioral, less patterned AI.

column1: In which genre do players prefer unpredictability, and why?
column2: Sports games: predictable patterns become exploitable holes.

column1: How do predatory mammals move, according to Rogers' nature guide?
column2: In looping arcs as they circle prey.

column1: Bruce Lee rule: dozens of enemies surround the hero but attack in ____.
column2: ones and twos

column1: Name the five pathing/behavior AI questions.
column2: How mobile, aggressive, team-player, defensive and versatile is the enemy?

column1: Why give enemies a sense of self-preservation?
column2: Cautious or cowardly enemies feel like real people.

column1: How do you fix waypoint enemies clipping corners?
column2: Pull the waypoints in a bit at corners and near objects.

column1: Name four enemy introduction techniques.
column2: Freeze/zoom camera, show the name, foreshadow, dramatic entrance.

column1: Which game foreshadows the licker by having it run past a window?
column2: Resident Evil 2.

column1: Players camp spawn points and kill enemies the instant they appear. Name fixes.
column2: Make enemies invulnerable while spawning, spawn them off-screen, or use a delivery mechanic (like Maximo's coffins).

column1: Fighting enemies is supposed to be ____.
column2: fun

column1: What does an enemy's death/removal style affect besides feel?
column2: The game's age rating (ESRB).

column1: Why is the charging exploder enemy bad design?
column2: Cameras rarely show it coming, so there's no fair warning; its only answer is avoidance.

column1: Enemies should be ____, not avoided.
column2: fought

column1: Name the six reasons to make players want to fight.
column2: Loot, they block the path, they have the key, take their power, they taunt you, it makes you feel badass.

column1: Name the four enemy attack families.
column2: Melee, weapon combat, projectile combat, persistent damage.

column1: What is a 'tell'?
column2: An animation (or sound) warning that an attack is coming, e.g., cocking a fist or a laser sight locking on.

column1: Name the ten non-damaging grief tools.
column2: Block/parry, knockback, stun, freeze/paralyze/capture, repair/heal, buff, thief, leech, unexpected behaviors, vulnerabilities/resistances.

column1: Why is knockback especially effective on narrow platforms?
column2: It can knock the player off, even to their death.

column1: How does freeze differ from stun?
column2: The player can break out of a freeze by button mashing or stick wiggling.

column1: Your async raid design lets attackers steal a defender's purchased item. Which rule is broken?
column2: Thief rule: never steal anything bought or earned through progression; only replaceable things.

column1: What does a leech drain?
column2: Charged-up resources: super meter, mana, shield power, fuel.

column1: How should vulnerabilities and resistances be designed?
column2: Clear and logical (snow creature weak to fire); never leave players wondering why something failed.

column1: Where do you start when balancing enemy health?
column2: With how many hits it should take to die, considering all the hero's attacks.

column1: What is the 'Red Ninja/Blue Ninja' principle?
column2: Reuse assets, but enemies with different behaviors must look different at a glance.

column1: Which Mortal Kombat duo began as reskins of each other?
column2: Sub-Zero and Scorpion.

column1: Name the two starting points for inventing your own enemies.
column2: Your theme (environment) or your story (main enemy/arch-nemesis).

column1: Why use stereotypical evil visuals like red eyes and spikes?
column2: Stereotypes are instantly readable, so players know to attack.

column1: What is a villain's 'Joker moment'?
column2: A scene where the villain does something truly evil, like executing a henchman, to prove how bad they are.

column1: How did Demolition Man keep its villain Simon present?
column2: He ran onscreen at the start of every level, shook his fist at the player and ran off.

column1: Why should villainy impact gameplay, not just story?
column2: Losing a blacksmith, healer or storage hurts the player directly, so they truly hate the enemy.

column1: Why not kill the boss at the end of every fight?
column2: A recurring villain builds history and more hatred, and leaves someone to fight later.

column1: What did Maximo's skeleton do after hitting the player, and why?
column2: A gunslinger-style sword flourish, giving the player an opening to strike back.

column1: Name the four non-enemy enemies.
column2: Gremlin, tormentor, time, human competitor.

column1: What is a gremlin enemy?
column2: Looks like an enemy but undoes the player's progress instead of fighting (e.g., SimCity's monster).

column1: A boss is a large and/or challenging enemy that blocks the player's ____ and is the climax of a level or world.
column2: progression

column1: Why must the player's moveset be finished before you design a boss?
column2: Bosses are built around the player's moves (learned moves) or a new ability; change the moveset and the boss breaks.

column1: Name the three boss design approaches.
column2: Learned moves, new abilities, combination (emphasize one).

column1: Your event's mastermind is beaten, but you want one last climax that isn't a person. Which Bond boss type fits?
column2: The global threat (e.g., a doomsday timer or device).

column1: What does Rogers suggest as a source of villain motivations?
column2: The Seven Deadly Sins: lust, gluttony, greed, sloth, wrath, envy, pride.

column1: Why should defeating the villain give the hero knowledge rather than treasure or power?
column2: In the Hero's Journey the hero returns changed, with knowledge; loot alone is a shallow payoff.

column1: What's wrong with a camera that's too low in a boss fight?
column2: Foreshortening hides distance and incoming attacks, and it can clip through geometry.

column1: What is 'crotch whacking'?
column2: When the hero is only tall enough to hit a huge boss in the crotch; avoid it with elevation.

column1: Name the four components of a boss fight.
column2: Primary attack, invulnerable attack, vulnerable state, opportunities.

column1: Why end a boss's vulnerable state with an attack or event like an electric burst?
column2: It pushes the player away and clearly signals the attack window is over.

column1: Why avoid fully random boss movement patterns?
column2: Players can't read them and get frustrated if they don't luck into a favorable one.

column1: Let the player administer the ____.
column2: coup de grace (the final blow)

column1: What is a false kill?
column2: Knocking an escaping boss to its knees first, holding the camera, so the player clearly wins before it flees.

column1: What should happen when a player dies in a boss fight?
column2: Safe respawn, boss waits until they're ready, and ideally the boss keeps its state instead of restarting.

column1: Name the two basic boss arena layouts.
column2: A circular arena or a linear screen-wide walkway.

column1: Your boss can't be damaged directly; players must lure it into electrified machines. What kind of boss is it?
column2: A puzzle boss.

column1: Name the four lessons of Paul Guirao's knife-fight boss.
column2: Drama over scale; intimacy creates urgency; reuse existing assets; tell story through the fight, not cutscenes.

column1: Your survivor-like's new enemy is small, fast AND deals huge damage. Which principle is violated?
column2: The Three Ss (speed, size, strength trade off); it will feel cheap.

column1: Players skip your optional elite enemies entirely. Which rule and fix apply?
column2: Enemies should be fought, not avoided: add a reason (loot, key, power) or make them less cheap.

column1: Your match-3 blocker variant looks identical to the old one but now spreads. What principle fixes the confusion?
column2: Red Ninja/Blue Ninja: new behavior needs a new look at a glance.

column1: Playtesters keep getting hit by a boss's slam 'out of nowhere.' What's missing?
column2: Telegraphing: a clear tell (wind-up, ground marker, sound) before the attack.

column1: Your event boss dies in an auto-playing cutscene after the last hit. What's the problem?
column2: It robs the player of the coup de grace; let them land the final blow and savor it.

column1: Players who fail your boss level must replay all three phases. What could you change?
column2: Keep the boss's state on respawn/continue so the fight resumes where it left off.

column1: Your raid boss feels stale by week three of reruns. Which chapter idea helps?
column2: Arenas with dynamic, reactive elements so each fight plays out differently.

column1: Your RPG's healer enemy feels unfair. What two fixes does Rogers suggest?
column2: Use healing sparingly with a visible animation and health bar, and let players interrupt the heal.

column1: What are Rogers' four types of level 'stuff'?
column2: Mechanics, hazards, props, puzzles.

column1: In board games, what does 'mechanics' mean?
column2: Rule systems: turns, action points, resource management, bidding, dice rolling.

column1: In video games (per Rogers), what is a mechanic?
column2: An object that creates gameplay when the player interacts with it (jump on, activate, push).

column1: Name four common video-game mechanics from the chapter.
column2: Any four: doors, pushable blocks, switches/levers, slippery floors, conveyor belts, moving platforms.

column1: Why should door-opening match the character?
column2: It expresses personality (Kratos kicks, Soap explodes, Jill creeps) and sets how entry plays.

column1: What did early Resident Evil's door animation secretly do?
column2: Hid level loading while building tension.

column1: Once you've decided how doors work, what's the rule?
column2: Keep the method of entry consistent throughout the whole game.

column1: What must a locked door communicate?
column2: Clearly why it can't be opened (unbreakable metal, a big lock, immovable debris).

column1: Three must-dos for switches and levers?
column2: Make them visible (glow/icon), show their effect (camera/voice/sound), show their new state (color/position/shape).

column1: What sound cue should a resetting switch use?
column2: A ticking timer sound, optionally with a timer graphic showing time left.

column1: What sound cue suits a one-way switch?
column2: A meaty sound signaling a permanent state change.

column1: What makes a crank different from a lever?
column2: It takes time to activate (hold, mash, or rhythm), and can be turned into a combat puzzle.

column1: What separates a hazard from an enemy?
column2: Intelligence and/or mobility: hazards have predictable patterns and limited movement.

column1: Rule #1 of hazard design?
column2: Make it look dangerous (spiky, flaming, icy, sparking, poisonous).

column1: Why did Rogers' hazard end up red instead of bee-striped?
column2: Red is a widely understood danger color; 'bees are dangerous' logic isn't clear to players.

column1: Difficulty promotes ____; challenge promotes ____.
column2: pain and loss; skill and improvement

column1: Why are instant-death hazards bad design?
column2: They're cheap and mean. Death should come from the player's own inattention or timing, and death is a poor teacher.

column1: What is the 'fun curve'?
column2: Rogers' term for the point where challenge tips into difficulty and frustration; never go over it.

column1: What's Rogers' fix for going over the fun curve?
column2: Ramping gameplay: build each system on the last, teach, master, then combine and gently intensify.

column1: Four rules of a timing puzzle?
column2: Readable pattern, predictable timing, tight-but-possible window with leeway, world tells.

column1: Why is random timing unfair in a timing puzzle?
column2: Players must learn the pattern to succeed; randomness makes learning impossible.

column1: Name three kinds of 'tells' for timing hazards.
column2: Any three: bloodstains, floor grooves, light/shadow, sound, particles, geometry, decorations.

column1: Which game may have had the first video-game timing puzzle, per Rogers' footnote?
column2: Dragon's Lair (spinning paddles in the Spectre chamber).

column1: What are props?
column2: Objects that don't move unless the player interacts; they make levels feel real and can serve as obstacles or cover.

column1: When should you stop a prop brainstorm?
column2: When ideas get silly or filthy: rest a day or two or do research.

column1: What's the risk of making everything breakable for loot?
column2: Gameplay turns into a mindless smash-fest.

column1: What is 'start to crate'?
column2: Old Man Murray's satirical metric: time until a game shows its first crate; a gauge of creativity.

column1: What's the rarest type of mechanic?
column2: The just-for-fun one (player piano, flushing toilet).

column1: In Rogers' chili metaphor, hazards are the ____.
column2: beans (filler that also makes 'music')

column1: What is flow?
column2: Csíkszentmihályi's state between boredom and too-much-difficulty: absorbed, energized, focused, losing track of time.

column1: In the Peter and the Wolf analogy, what does the cat (clarinet) represent?
column2: Hazards (conflict).

column1: In the Peter and the Wolf analogy, what does the bird (flute) represent?
