column2: Treasure and collectibles.

column1: What's step 7 of the orchestration recipe?
column2: Twist one element on its head to keep players on their toes.

column1: In the pit + enemy combo, where do you place the enemy?
column2: Far enough away that it doesn't engage until the player has landed safely.

column1: Why should the saw blade also kill enemies?
column2: Players feel clever luring enemies in; traps can be turned against their makers.

column1: Which two developers does Rogers cite for getting the most from few mechanics?
column2: Treasure and Naughty Dog.

column1: What's the baseball-pitcher lesson?
column2: Rotate mechanics in and out so they stay fresh; overuse bores players.

column1: Pros and cons of invisible checkpoints?
column2: Pro: no immersion break. Con: unclear when one is triggered or where you'll respawn.

column1: Why respawn players on the ground?
column2: So they don't wait to land (and avoid long respawn animations).

column1: Rogers' puzzle definition?
column2: A puzzle is a challenge that has a right answer.

column1: Why did Rogers drop 'fun' from Scott Kim's definition?
column2: Fun is subjective; challenging the player is the puzzle's real job.

column1: Show 'em the ____ and then send 'em after the ____.
column2: door; key

column1: What was wrong with Resident Evil 2's chess-piece puzzle?
column2: Arbitrary and unrelated to the story (chess pieces in a police station); ID cards would have fit.

column1: Four ways to solve a puzzle?
column2: Reason, knowledge, skill, dumb luck.

column1: How should the game handle a player who can't solve a puzzle?
column2: No big deal: offer hints or the answer at a mild cost, never a life, and let the player choose to pay.

column1: Progression is a ____, not a ____.
column2: right; reward

column1: Which game series is Rogers' example of diminishing rewards for hints?
column2: Professor Layton.

column1: What does 'no cat mustaches' warn against?
column2: Overclever, nonsensical Rube Goldberg solutions; it's player vs. puzzle, not designer vs. player.

column1: How many words did Scribblenauts recognize?
Minimum number of options for multiple-choice questions?
column2: Three.

column1: Max session length for a minigame per Rogers?
column2: 5–10 minutes (microgames: seconds).

column1: Why add a 'Ready?' screen when mixing a minigame into the core game?
column2: To give players a 'brain shift' between play styles.

column1: Five reasons Whack-a-Mole is a creative dead end?
column2: Reaction-only, random, repetitive, minimal input, endless.

column1: A match-3 level is tuned so most players lose by one move, then a gem continue pops. Which principle is violated?
column2: No rocks on the player's head / challenge, not difficulty: failure is engineered, not earned.

column1: Your new blocker and new booster launch in the same level and testers are confused. Which principle helps?
column2: Orchestration: introduce one new element at a time, then combine.

column1: Players respawn after a continue right in front of the obstacle that killed them. Which rule is broken?
column2: Checkpoint rule: never respawn next to a hazard.

column1: Your word game's hint costs a full life. What's the Rogers fix?
column2: Make the cost mild (coins or bonus), optional, and never a life.

column1: Players skip your locked feature because they don't know why it's locked. What fixes it?
column2: Make the lock obvious and say what opens it (e.g., 'Unlocks at Level 12').

column1: A timed boost has no countdown on screen and players feel cheated when it ends. What principle applies?
column2: Resetting-switch rule: show a timer graphic and an expiry cue.

column1: Every level in your game uses all 12 blockers and players say it feels samey. What's the fix?
column2: Rotate mechanics like pitchers: use subsets so each level has its own personality.

column1: Why does Rogers prefer red over 'clever' color schemes for hazards?
column2: Players must read danger instantly; widely understood signals beat artistic cleverness.

column1: Why should players be able to see that a puzzle piece was adjusted and reset it?
column2: It's easy to lose track of progress; visible state and a reset keep the focus on the puzzle, not confusion.

column1: Why give a stuck player multiple paths of progression?
column2: Puzzles are gates; side paths let them keep playing and return later, maybe with the answer.

column1: Why should executing a puzzle solution be quick after the A-Ha moment?
column2: The reward is the insight; after that, execution is just grunt work and shouldn't drag.

column1: Why limit minigame controls to a few buttons with one action each?
column2: Minigames imply easy-to-learn play; simple controls keep them a fun variety break, not a chore.

column1: Why does Rogers prefer challenging games to difficult ones if you want completion?
column2: Only a minority finish difficult games; challenge rewards skill and keeps most players progressing.

column1: Your hazard is a neon-pink cloud that players walk into because it looks like candy. Which rule is broken?
column2: Hazards must look dangerous (shape, color, sound, particles).

column1: Your puzzle needs an item found three zones away. Players give up. Which Rogers rule applies?
column2: Keep the tools needed to solve a puzzle nearby.

column1: Your merge game's event minigame lasts 20 minutes with complex controls. What would Rogers say?
column2: Keep minigames simple and short: 5–10 minutes max, few controls.

column1: Your ad shows a pull-the-pin puzzle that isn't in the game. What's the problem?
column2: Misleading creative: the minigame should actually exist in the game (regulators have ruled against such ads).

column1: Your level's opening asks players to 'find 5 gears' without saying why. Which motto fixes it?
column2: Show 'em the door, then send 'em after the key: reveal the goal and reward first.

column1: Players say your blade-trap arena is just annoying. What design twist from the book could make it fun?
column2: Let the trap kill enemies too, so players can lure them in and feel clever.

column1: A puzzle is a ____ that has a right answer.
column2: challenge

column1: Rogers' footnote insists: walking is not ____.
column2: gameplay

column1: In the Peter and the Wolf analogy, when does the wolf (enemies) enter, and what happens to the music afterwards?
column2: Only after every other instrument is already playing (movement, treasure, mechanics, hazards are familiar). Then the music keeps intensifying through the fight until the hunters' drums rescue everyone: a rising fight with a big payoff.

column1: According to Rogers, what is the goal of good level design, and what does reaching it feel like?
column2: Helping the player reach flow (Csíkszentmihályi). It feels like making music: a natural rhythm of moving and acting emerges as the player crosses the level.

column1: What are the two defining traits of a power-up's effect?
column2: Immediate and (usually) temporary.

column1: Name the four categories of power-ups.
column2: Defensive, offensive, movement, game changers.

column1: What four pickup methods does Rogers' distance diagram show?
column2: Walk over, actively pick up, auto-attract within a radius, proximity activation.

column1: Name four expiry cues for a temporary power-up.
column2: HUD element, visual cue, sound cue, music cue (or it lasts until you lose a life).

column1: If health-ups refill different amounts, what's the rule?
column2: Make them look different.

column1: Invulnerability vs. invincibility?
column2: Both block enemy damage; invincibility also destroys enemies on contact (often not bosses).

column1: Why should invulnerable players still be affected by physics/geometry hazards like falls?
column2: Otherwise collision detection problems arise.

column1: How do protective power-ups differ from invulnerability/invincibility?
column2: They can usually be upgraded, modified and extended, and may have their own health meter.

column1: What is an 'indirect attack' power-up?
column2: A fire-and-forget trap dropped behind you (smokescreen, oil slick, bomb), common in kart and car-combat games.

column1: What does a smart bomb do?
column2: Clears the screen when things get too tough or the player needs a breather.

column1: What's a multi-weapon power-up?
column2: One that improves your current weapon without fundamentally changing it (e.g., Contra's 5-shot spread).

column1: What was Galaga's companion twist?
column2: A captured ship became your companion: you lost a life but gained double shot.

column1: Why must movement power-ups be considered when setting player metrics?
column2: They change speed, reach and size, which can break gaps, jumps and level layouts.

column1: What's the usual trade-off of a speed power-up?
column2: Less control, because faster reactions are needed.

column1: What three things does Super Mario Bros.' super mushroom give?
column2: Bigger size, one extra hit, and the ability to break bricks.

column1: What does a 'change state' power-up do? Give the classic example.
column2: Flips the play dynamic: Pac-Man's power pellet turns the hunted into the hunter.

column1: Why are magnetic power-ups useful?
column2: They pull treasure to you, removing risk and post-fight cleanup.

column1: Two rules for mobile (moving) power-ups?
column2: Never faster than the player; never immune to a magnetic power-up.

column1: When are conditional power-ups OK?
column2: When the conditions are clear to the player (e.g., Maximo's full-armor-set power).

column1: Why use anti-power-ups sparingly?
column2: They're only fun once or twice.

column1: Rogers' version of 'love thy player'?
column2: The designer is a gentle hand on the player's rear, pushing them upward.

column1: What does DDB adjust?
column2: Challenge and rewards, based on player performance.

column1: In Rogers' DDB example, what comes out of a chest when you're low on health?
column2: A health-up (otherwise treasure).

column1: Why does Rogers dislike automatic difficulty reduction?
column2: Many players find it insulting; better to offer the choice.

column1: What is rubberbanding?
column2: Opponents slow down when the player falls far behind so they can catch up.

column1: IF YOUR GUT SAYS A LEVEL IS OVERLONG, TOO TOUGH, OR DULL, THEN ____.
column2: IT PROBABLY IS

column1: What are designer blinders?
column2: After endless play, designers need much harder content to feel challenged than real players do.

column1: Which game does Rogers cite for autosaving when loading new areas?
column2: Fallout 3.

column1: Why is 'the player must die three times' bad design?
column2: Player death should never be a design yardstick; punishing with death is negative reinforcement.

column1: What went wrong with Maximo's mimic chest?
column2: Players began dreading every chest; it was fun for the designer, not the player.

column1: How would Rogers fix a mimic enemy?
column2: Give clues (a color change, wobbling pots like Zelda: Spirit Tracks).

column1: What are the two most powerful tools to keep players playing?
column2: Greed and reward.

column1: NEVER UNDERESTIMATE THE ____ OF THE PLAYER.
column2: GREED

column1: What's the 'me too' factor?
column2: Keeping up with the Joneses: wanting what other players have (Rogers' WoW robot chicken).

column1: What treasure-placement guideline did Maximo use?
column2: Buried treasure next to trees (or pillars/gravestones if there were no trees).

column1: What are Half-Life's four steps for introducing an item?
column2: Hear about it, see it held, see it used, then get and use it.

column1: Why does Half-Life's item introduction work?
column2: By the time players get the item, they know what it is and does, and they want it.

column1: You can't have a game without a victory condition, and never a victory without a ____.
column2: reward

column1: Rogers' four reward rules?
column2: Show early; reward soon, often, with variety and surprise; celebrate wins with fanfare; make rewards matter.

column1: What's 'the best reward'?
column2: The one the player didn't know they needed until they got it.

column1: List the 10 reward types.
column2: Scoring, achievements, treasure, loot, power-ups, souvenirs, bonus materials, praise, surprise, progression.

column1: What revived scoring in the early 2000s?
column2: Browser games (Bejeweled, Feeding Frenzy) and online leaderboards (Xbox Live, PSN).

column1: Achievements are high scores with ____.
column2: personality

column1: Why publish achievement lists before release?
column2: They act as a to-do list and point players toward ideas they'd never try.

column1: Example escalating treasure denominations?
column2: 1, 5, 10, 50, 100, without spreading them too far apart.

column1: What's a 'virtual penny'?
column2: Treasure so low-value no one bothers picking it up.

column1: Rogers' four rarity tiers?
column2: Common, uncommon, rare, unique.

column1: Why offer a choice between two really good items?
column2: Delicious agony now, plus a reason to come back next time.

column1: If players should afford $300 of items, how much treasure goes in the level?
column2: At least $300.

column1: What's the risk of regenerating treasure?
column2: Players can mine/farm levels and break the economy.

column1: Why show all buyable items early (e.g., an ability tree)?
column2: Players can plan how to spend their money.

column1: Why not make treasure designs too diverse?
column2: Players may mistake treasure for power-ups.

column1: Encumbrance rule for shopping?
column2: Never make players shuttle cash from storage to the store; charge their account.

column1: Name the ten shopkeeper categories.
column2: Offense, defense, repairs, replenishable resources, skills, access, vanity, whimsy, information, saves.

column1: THE BEST REWARDS ARE ____.
column2: HARD WON

column1: Loot vs. bought items: which should be better?
column2: Found loot; save the best weapons, armor and guns for loot.

column1: Two presentation rules for souvenirs?
column2: A tight camera/viewer to admire them and a label saying where they were found.

column1: Why give souvenirs special properties (dragon boots vs rug)?
column2: Useful souvenirs carry more meaning, show off your feat, and make players chase the next encounter.

column1: When should bonus materials be designed and built?
column2: Designed early, built late, so you can judge what feels like a bonus.

column1: When should cheats be enabled per Rogers?
column2: Only after the player has played through the game once.

column1: What's the warning about praise?
column2: Praise loses meaning if given for nothing or trivial acts.

column1: What's the point of the Pirate's Lair skeleton?
column2: A pure surprise-and-fun reward with no purpose but a laugh; games should include such moments.

column1: Your match-3 sells boosters, but players say levels feel impossible without them. Which principle is at risk?
column2: Love thy player / no 'die three times' design: boosters should feel like help, not ransom.

column1: Rewards in your RPG are random filler unrelated to the next challenge. What's the Rogers fix?
column2: Make rewards matter: solve the last problem and give an edge on the next.

column1: Players farm one easy level for infinite coins and prices feel trivial. Which section applies?
column2: Regenerating treasure lets players mine levels: add caps or diminishing returns.

column1: Your F2P shop sells the strongest weapons only for gems. Which Rogers rule conflicts?
column2: The best rewards are hard won: found/earned loot should beat bought items (avoid pay-to-win).

column1: Your team finds the new event 'medium' but players quit at stage 3. What's likely happening?
column2: Designer blinders: test with fresh players and cut what's too hard or boring.

column1: Players never notice your new hero. How could Half-Life's method help?
column2: Have characters mention it, show it held and used (showcase/trial) before players get it.

column1: Your level-clear screen is a plain 'Complete' label. What would Rogers add?
column2: Massive fanfare: sounds, particles, character celebration, camera moves, praise layers.

column1: Your coin trail leads players into a hidden spike pit for laughs. What principle does this violate?
column2: Use greed for good, not to lure players to their deaths.

column1: Your gacha shows no odds and has no guarantee. Which F2P best practices are missing?
column2: Published odds (store requirement), a pity system, and duplicate value.

column1: A boost silently expires and players feel robbed. Which design question was skipped?
column2: Expiry cues: what tells the player a temporary power-up is about to run out.

column1: Why do power-ups need a clear visual identity (glow, strobe, rotate, bounce)?
column2: So they stand out in the world and players instantly recognize them, and aren't confused with treasure.

column1: Why does rubberbanding make racing games better?
column2: Racing alone on an empty track is no fun; keeping opponents close keeps the race tense.

column1: Why use greed 'for good' instead of luring players into traps?
column2: Trapping players just proves the designer is clever; using greed to motivate fights, collections and exploration keeps them playing.

column1: Why should trailers and similar bonus extras always be skippable?
column2: Forcing players to watch wastes their time and breeds resentment; optional extras feel like gifts.

column1: Your runner's jetpack lets players skip half the obstacles and break level pacing. What did the designers forget?
column2: To account for movement power-ups when designing player metrics and layouts.

column1: Players ignore your 1-coin pickups because upgrades cost 50,000. Which rule applies?
column2: Avoid virtual pennies: keep denominations meaningful relative to prices.

column1: Your shop shows the same 6 items forever and visits drop. What's Rogers' fix?
column2: Stock variety and rotate the selection (offer two great choices, some out of reach).

column1: Players complain their streak broke because of a bad Wi-Fi day and they quit. What F2P fix echoes Rogers' 'love thy player'?
column2: Add streak protection or grace days (a defensive power-up for habits).

column1: The designer should be the gentle ____ on the player's rear, pushing them ever upwards.
column2: hand

column1: Give the player a personal space to show off trophies; once the shelves fill, they'll want to ____.
column2: catch them all (collect the full set)

column1: Which Rogers-favorite achievement rewards doing nothing for 5 minutes, and in which game?
column2: You've wasted your life in Saw: an ironic, joke achievement for being idle.

column1: What does the Team Fortress 2 "Be polite" achievement ask for?
column2: Tipping your hat so the freeze-cam shot the enemy sees after you kill them shows it (taunting politely).

column1: How does Brutal Legend's "Six degrees of Schaefer" work?
column2: You must play with or against anyone who has it, so the chain links back to creator Tim Schafer: a viral, social achievement.

column1: How many praise layers does Zak & Wiki fire for a solved puzzle, and what are the first four for any correct action?
column2: Eight in total. Any correct action: success sting, funny hero reaction, hero particle effect, Wiki's text congrats with his own sting and particles. Puzzle adds a yellow star burst, a longer tune, a "look at me" item pose, and the item name.

column1: How were God of War's Challenge of the Gods minigames cheap to build?
column2: Everything was already in the game code; they only gave players different victory conditions (re-contextualize your most fun gameplay).

column1: What does Rogers advise for alternate endings?
column2: Make sure players know other endings exist; match good and evil evenly; give ways to course-correct between outcomes; let the player choose the outcome, not the game.

column1: Name four ways to upgrade a lazy art-viewer slideshow.
column2: Artist commentary or music, show environments/props/maps/design docs, player-controlled pacing, a magnifier, a hidden reward, or collect-the-pieces puzzle art with a payout.

column1: Why should cheats stay locked until the player has finished the game once?
column2: Otherwise players cheat themselves out of the intended experience; some games reinforce this (no good ending, GTA brands you a cheater, TF2 hands non-cheaters the cheater's lament halo).

column1: What fanfare elements does Rogers suggest for a win?
column2: Fireworks, dramatic camera pans, the hero jumping for joy, cheering crowds, slot-machine sounds, and lots of particles and visual effects.

column1: Why are model viewers especially good in RTS games?
column2: Characters are normally seen from a distant camera, so pan/rotate/zoom viewers let players admire the models up close.

column1: In Rogers' arena example, what changes between a 10-minute fight and a 30-minute fight?
column2: Ten minutes is survivable with enough health and modest skill; at thirty, fatigue and attrition set in and the player probably loses: length is a difficulty dial.

column1: Name four non-money treasures Rogers cites and the one requirement.
column2: Bolts (Ratchet & Clank), studs (Lego games), souls (God of War), bottle caps (Fallout). It must sparkle and make a satisfying cha-ching when collected.

column1: Name three "little moments" Rogers cites besides the Pirate's Lair skeleton.
column2: Stan Lee's cameo in Marvel: Ultimate Alliance 2, Ape Escape monkeys in Metal Gear Solid 3's jungle, Braid's homage to Mario's World 1-1.

column1: How does Fable stroke the player's ego?
column2: NPCs recoil in horror or compliment the hero depending on alignment, rewarding the time spent being good or evil.

column1: Name three shop settings Rogers suggests instead of a generic store.
column2: Vending machines (Borderlands, BioShock), a garage for a racing game, a sporting goods shop for a sports game: the store adds character and theme.

column1: What did playing Gauntlet with friends teach Rogers about co-op games?
column2: A cooperative game can easily dissolve into a competitive one when there are scarce resources to grab.

column1: What is head-to-head multiplayer?
column2: Two or more players competing in real time on the same game system.

column1: What is the difference between LAN and WAN play?
column2: Proximity: LAN covers a room, office or campus; WAN (the Internet) extends beyond.

column1: What is a client server in multiplayer?
column2: A computer big and fast enough to handle many users at once, used by MMOs and MMORPGs.

column1: The three play styles are competitive, cooperative and ____.
column2: conjugate

column1: What is conjugate gameplay?
column2: Players share the same play space but not the same goals.

column1: In a death match, how do players usually start?
column2: On common ground, then gain or lose equipment that gives an edge.

column1: Why are fighting games often played head-to-head rather than online?
column2: Network lag interrupts the split-second timing fighting needs.

column1: What makes area/territory control exciting?
column2: The tug-of-war of attacking, retreating and retaking as you move the line toward the final area.

column1: How does king of the hill differ from area control?
column2: One team is given a location and must defend it for a set period of time.

column1: In capture the flag, how does a player become the target?
column2: By holding an object (flag, oddball skull) or being designated 'it' by the game.

column1: For combat races, use a ____ system where the leader is most vulnerable.
column2: regressive

column1: What did Burnout Paradise's Easy Drive mode add?
column2: Multiple drivers could join events and socialize while driving.

column1: What is Man vs God mode?
column2: One player is God controlling almost everything; the other is Man with limited resources trying to survive.

column1: What should gambling modes avoid?
column2: Progressive systems, where early winners snowball and everyone behind falls further back.

column1: Why are creation modes great for a game's lifespan?
column2: Players create content for you, extending the game's life and spawning new play patterns.

column1: How many community-made levels did LittleBigPlanet: Game of the Year Edition showcase?
Name three virtual-life examples from the book.
column2: PlayStation Home, Second Life, Animal Crossing.

column1: Why does Street Fighter break with more than two players?
column2: Players bunch up, are hard to see, collision detection struggles, and it becomes mob warfare instead of a skill contest.

column1: Roughly how many players per server does the book give for World of Warcraft?
The right number of players is ____.
column2: whatever is right for your game

column1: What is buffing?
column2: Spell casting that affects the entire party, letting players take on roles (e.g., a healing cleric).

column1: What crafting failure should you never allow?
column2: Destroying a hard-to-get, expensive item; it punishes the player twice.

column1: Why let players craft items themselves?
column2: The items become recognizably 'their creations', which builds attachment.

column1: What should an MMO economy balance?
column2: The effort spent earning money vs the items it can buy.

column1: What does the book say is the main reason players quit an MMO?
column2: The grind.

column1: What does the Mafia Wars example show?
column2: Stacking item gates and random drops between player and goal makes progress feel artificially slowed and frustrating.

column1: Why are dungeons instanced?
column2: Each group gets its own (often randomized) copy, so several groups can play at once and nobody waits for a restock.

column1: Rarity scheme: common, uncommon, ____, unique.
column2: rare

column1: Name two ways to gate an 'open' world.
column2: Level or gear requirements; or let players wander in and get beaten until they retreat and level up.

column1: What is griefing and how should you fight it?
column2: Harassing a player by repeatedly killing them; use systems, clear rules and a warning/zero-tolerance policy.

column1: Name the four guild tools Rogers suggests.
column2: Communication tools, stat tracking, raid calendars, guild asset customization.

column1: Why give players housing?
column2: A home base to show off achievements makes them feel at home and want to return again and again.

column1: Two ways MMOs protect players who don't want PvP?
column2: Dedicated PvP servers, or PvP only in certain locations.

column1: How should raid loot be shared?
column2: Easily, based on each player's performance.

column1: What is spawn camping?
column2: Waiting at a spawn point to kill players or enemies as they appear.

column1: Players will always do the ____ thing you expect.
column2: last

column1: Your async attack game sees new players quitting after being raided 5 times in an hour. Which book problem and fix?
column2: Griefing / spawn camping: add safeguards like a shield after being attacked or per-target cooldowns.

column1: In your PvP game, players who buy power packs win every match and free players quit. Which book rule did you break?
column2: Avoid progressive rich-get-richer systems; keep competition fair (match by power, sell cosmetics/speed).

column1: Your gear upgrade can fail and destroy the legendary item used. Players rage. Which principle?
column2: Don't punish twice: never destroy hard-to-get, expensive inputs on failure.

column1: Your clan boss event only rewards the top damage dealer, and casual members stop joining. What does the book's raid advice suggest?
column2: Make raids beatable by varied teams and share loot by each player's performance (plus a participation floor).

column1: Your new 50-player mode has 4-minute queues in small regions. Which principle?
column2: The right number is what your game (and its matchmaking pool) can support; reduce player count or add bots.

column1: Async or sync: which suits a casual audience playing in 2-minute bursts on bad connections?
column2: Async: play anytime, no queue, tolerant of connection drops.

column1: Why do help requests (troop donations, life requests) boost retention?
column2: Tiny effort creates reciprocity, belonging and a reason to open the app; quitting means leaving friends.

column1: Which mode is the closest to single-player with co-op?
column2: Survival.

column1: You want a mode where a newbie and a veteran clanmate can play together without the veteran stomping. Which play style should you pick?
column2: Cooperative (same objective, working together), ideally a team objective mode.

column1: Your clan feature launched with chat only; leaders complain they cannot see who contributes or when wars happen. Which book advice applies?
column2: Build guild tools: stat tracking and calendars (plus communication and customization).

column1: In the Mafia Wars grind example, what chain of requirements sits behind the 'Extort a Corrupt Judge' job?
column2: Blackmail photos (earned in 'Take Compromising Photo') -> a disposable camera -> either gifted by other players or dropped in 'Rob an Electronics Store', with no guaranteed drop.

column1: How does the book describe the way MMOs cope with enormous traffic under the client-server connection type?
column2: A big, fast server (many of them) working with many LANs to meet the user demand.

column1: Which character-creation logic does Rogers reuse to justify letting players craft their own items?
column2: Just like creating characters, what the player makes themselves becomes recognizable as 'their creation', so they bond with it.

column1: What do auction houses add to MMO trading, and what should trading in general be?
column2: Regular auctions where players bid on items with in-game treasure. Trading should be simple and scam-proof, with places in the world that promote it.

column1: In capture the flag, what happens to the target player, and how does the cooperative version work?
column2: The player who is 'it' is sometimes handicapped while carrying the object; in the cooperative version teammates protect that player.

column1: Give Rogers' player counts for Street Fighter, Power Stone, Uno, LittleBigPlanet, Burnout Paradise, Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2 and MAG.
column2: Street Fighter 2; Power Stone 4; Uno 4; LittleBigPlanet 4; Burnout Paradise 8; Modern Warfare 2 16; MAG 64, 128 or 256 depending on mode. (WoW: roughly 4,000-5,000 per server.)

column1: What is a 'drop', and which other special-item sources does the book list for item collection?
column2: A drop is an item gained only by defeating specific creatures. Others: seasonal items available only at certain times of year, and items earned by attending world events.

column1: What did testing the Star Tours ride reveal?
column2: Without John Williams' Star Wars theme it didn't feel like Star Wars; the theme was added.

column1: Why is music usually left until late in production?
column2: It requires a lot of work and coordination among many team members.

column1: What is Red Book audio?
column2: The set of standards for CD audio, which let game music sound like any recorded music.

column1: What are the two kinds of game music?
column2: Licensed and original.

column1: Who usually handles music licensing deals for a game?
column2: The game's publisher.

column1: What range of per-song license fees does the book give (2010)?
column2: About $2,500 to over $30,000 per song.

column1: Game music buyouts typically last from 7 years to ____.
column2: life of product

column1: Name two cheaper alternatives to an expensive licensed song.
column2: A cover version (like the first Guitar Hero) or a similar-sounding music library track.

column1: What does a music director do?
column2: Creates the music and handles performing, recording and preparing it for the game.

column1: Why did Rogers give his Maximo composer a mix tape?
column2: Concrete examples cut out guesswork about what each level should sound like.

column1: What is tempo?
column2: The speed of the music (walking pace = andante).

column1: Moving one octave up ____ the frequency.
column2: doubles (one octave down halves it)

column1: How can pitch add variety to game sounds?
column2: Shifting a sound's frequency (e.g., a sword clang) avoids identical repetition without new recordings.

column1: A ____ is three or more tones creating a harmony.
column2: chord

column1: What three things can a piece's mood be based on?
column2: Emotion, action, or location.

column1: What is a musical theme, per the book?
column2: The heart of the composition; composers usually write it first, then flesh it out.

column1: What's the risk of putting temp music into the build?
column2: The team gets attached to or tired of it, and unlicensed music left in can cost huge fees or force scrapping work.

column1: Why do background tracks loop?
column2: To save memory and composition time.

column1: How did Maximo vs. Army of Zin avoid music repetition on a budget?
column2: Two songs per world, alternated so the same one never played twice in a row.

column1: Why should your best piece of music go on the start screen?
column2: It is the first music players hear, sets the stage for the whole game and gets them excited to play.

column1: What is a dynamic score?
column2: Music broken into themes that play when certain situations arise (e.g., combat).

column1: What is a leitmotif?
column2: A specific musical theme associated with a character or scenario.

column1: Name the six common dynamic score themes.
column2: Mystery, warning, combat, chase/fast movement, victory, walking.

column1: What is a sting?
column2: A very short piece of music, e.g., to signal victory.

column1: Always make the music more exciting than the ____ on screen.
column2: action

column1: Why should walking music be faster than the walk?
column2: Slow music makes players move slowly; a faster beat motivates them to move faster.

column1: Why might a hub area use environmental effects instead of background music?
column2: Music can be overbearing or wrong for some places; ambient sound sets the mood (Maximo hubs used effects, levels used music).

column1: Name three things silence can convey.
column2: Great speed (Burnout boost), intense action (F.E.A.R. reflex time), suspense (or failed humor).

column1: When should you build the sound effects list?
column2: As you develop the move sets of characters and enemies, starting with the main character.

column1: Why are hit reaction sounds so important?
column2: Whenever players get hit, they need to know it.

column1: What two jobs do vocal cues do?
column2: Tell the player what's possible or accomplished, and add personality to the character.

column1: Positive events: make sounds go ____ in pitch and tempo.
column2: up (down for negative/failure)

column1: What is sweetening? Give the book example.
column2: Enhancing a sound that doesn't sound right in reality; bone breaks sweetened with a bowling ball hitting pins.

column1: What should you tell the sound programmer about an attack sound?
column2: Which animation frame it should play on (after timing is locked with animators).

column1: Local vs distant vs priority sounds?
column2: Local fades with distance; distant is heard from far away; priority always plays as gameplay feedback.

column1: Why must sound-based gameplay have visuals?
column2: More clues for everyone, and hearing-impaired players can play.

column1: What health risk do rhythm games carry, and the fix?
column2: Fatigue/injury from constant hand and wrist movement; mandatory breaks between songs or levels.

column1: Your puzzle game's 'out of moves' warning is only a beep. Testers on mute keep losing by surprise. Which principle?
column2: Don't rely on sound alone: echo important cues with visuals (and haptics).

column1: Coins collected from a chest all play the identical clink 40 times and testers find it grating. Fix?
column2: Use pitch variation (and voice limits) so repeated sounds vary.

column1: A soft-launch build still contains a pop song the team used as temp music. What's the danger?
column2: Using music without rights: possible huge fees or having to scrap work. Replace it before shipping.

column1: Your gacha reveal feels flat. Which two audio tools from the chapter could fix it?
column2: Silence/build-up before the reveal, then a victory sting with rising pitch (rarity-specific).

column1: During a boss fight, combos, coins, the boss roar and music all play at once and feedback gets lost. Which concept?
column2: Sound prioritization: make feedback sounds priority, limit and duck the rest.

column1: You want a villain's arrival to be recognized before players see him. Which tool?
column2: A leitmotif: a signature theme tied to the character.

column1: Short descriptive names like Lv2Song.wav help because ____.
column2: nobody has to guess what a file is

column1: Name two music-game families besides rhythm games.
column2: Short-term memory (Simon, PaRappa), pitch/singing (SingStar), music creation (Electroplankton, Fluid).

column1: Your sci-fi game team says an orchestral score feels too expected. What does the book allow?
column2: Go in another creative direction (hip-hop, trance, even polka), as long as it fits the experience.

column1: Players keep missing a hidden chest in a dark corner. Which sound technique could guide them (plus a visual)?
column2: Sound as a clue: a ticking, ringing or shimmering sound they can follow.

column1: Who helps you assign sounds to the local, distant and priority categories, and what problem does that solve?
column2: The sound programmer; it prevents cacophony from too many sounds playing at once.

column1: Which companies negotiate music licenses on behalf of publishers, and who usually handles the deal for a game?
column2: ASCAP and Third Element negotiate for the music publishers; the game's own publisher usually handles obtaining the rights.

column1: A free sound effect from the internet fits your trailer perfectly. What must you check before using it, and why?
column2: Its copyright and license; better to be sure up front than face a huge lawsuit later.

column1: Besides pitch, what else should rise to make a sound feel positive, and what does a negative sound do?
column2: Tempo as well as pitch goes up for positive moments (extra life, task done); negative or failure sounds go down.

column1: What is a cutscene?
column2: An animated or live-action sequence, usually without player control, used for story, spectacle, atmosphere, dialogue, character development and clues.

column1: Why are cutscenes a double-edged sword?
column2: They look fantastic, but many are too long, unnecessary or a chore, so players skip them.

column1: What question should you ask before making a cutscene?
column2: Can it be done in the game?

column1: Name the six types of cutscenes.
column2: FMV, animated, Flash-animated, prerendered, puppet show, scripted event.

column1: Who usually produces FMV cutscenes, and why?
column2: An outside production company, because FMV needs all the resources of a movie production.

column1: Why did FMV become less popular?
column2: Too expensive to produce for something the audience may not even watch.

column1: Name two mid-90s systems built around FMV games.
column2: Any two of: 3DO, Philips CD-i, Sega Mega CD (plus PCs).

column1: Why are animated (cel/stop-motion) cutscenes rare?
column2: Involved production, long shooting time and high cost.

column1: What gives Flash-animated cutscenes their distinctive style?
column2: Still images and simple movement.

column1: What are prerendered cutscenes made from?
column2: High-resolution versions of the game's models and environments, with cinematic cameras.

column1: Why are they called puppet shows?
column2: Early in-engine cutscene characters moved unnaturally, like marionettes.

column1: What visually separates a puppet show from gameplay?
column2: Only the use of a cinematic camera.

column1: How do scripted events differ from puppet shows?
column2: The player keeps limited to full interaction during the sequence.

column1: Why are scripted events the preferred storytelling method in FPS/action games?
column2: They convey story without upsetting the pace of gameplay.

column1: What is the Groundhog Day phenomenon?
column2: Replaying the same scripted event after dying, feeling stuck in a time loop.

column1: Name the four techniques to make sure players see a scripted event.
column2: Trigger when the player faces it; frame with level geometry; move the camera to show the space; start camera moves from the player's POV.

column1: What should the camera always show in an event?
column2: Clear cause and effect (pull this lever, that door opens).

column1: Step 1 of writing a screenplay?
column2: Outline the story: beginning, middle and end.

column1: What do you list for each scene in Step 2, and why?
column2: Characters and locations, for staging and asset creation.

column1: Why did SpongeBob: Atlantis SquarePantis start at the end of its story?
column2: It was the most action-packed scene; start with a bang.

column1: It's always better to have the player ____ than ____.
column2: do; watch

column1: Save cutscenes for ____ and ____ (big intimate and spectacular moments).
column2: kissing; explosions (blowing things up)

column1: What's the most important quality of game dialogue, per Step 4?
column2: Brevity: get the point across in as few words as possible.

column1: Screenplay scene heading: SCENE #. ____ / ____ — LOCATION — TIME OF DAY.
column2: INT. / EXT.

column1: In screenplay format, what goes in ALL CAPS in the description?
column2: Characters (when introduced) and action.

column1: Where does actor direction go in screenplay format?
column2: In parentheses under the character's name.

column1: Why read your dialogue out loud?
column2: Lines that sound fine in your head often sound strange or clunky spoken.

column1: What does Step 7 ask you to do?
column2: Let the script simmer a day or two and have someone else read it (without hovering).

column1: Why does every VO line need a file name?
column2: The sound engineer names the cut audio files with it, and the programmer uses the same file in the game.

column1: Voice actors read grunts ____, so write them how you want them to sound.
column2: literally

column1: Where can you learn to spell grunts and sound words?
column2: Comic books (onomatopoeia like POW, CRASH, AIIEEE).

column1: What is a temp track used for?
column2: Determining audio file size and length (timing and blocking).

column1: Never animate ____ to a temp track.
column2: lip sync

column1: Who should you hire before hiring voice actors?
column2: A voice director.

column1: Name four things a voice director does.
column2: Casts from your descriptions, books the studio/gets rates, schedules sessions, directs actors and works with sound techs.

column1: Why should the writer attend the voice session?
column2: Rewrites happen, and actors and the director don't always know a line's context.

column1: Your mobile game's 45-second intro cinematic can't be skipped, and many installs quit during it. Which truths apply?
column2: Allow skipping, keep cutscenes short, and tell the story through gameplay (do > watch).

column1: Players retrying a hard boss level must sit through its intro every time. Which problem?
column2: The Groundhog Day phenomenon: show it once, then skip on retries.

column1: Your tutorial explains boosters with a text popup, and players don't get it. Which staging principle helps?
column2: Show clear cause and effect: make them tap the booster and watch it clear the row (do, don't watch).

column1: Your animator synced a hero's lip movement to your own scratch recording; the pro actor's take doesn't match. Which rule was broken?
column2: Never lip-sync to a temp track; use it only for timing and blocking.

column1: An event story beat needs a castle collapsing, beyond what your meta screen can animate. What does the book suggest?
column2: That's a 'kissing and explosions' moment: one of the few beats worth a short cutscene.

column1: Your localization team keeps mixing up which line goes where. Which step fixes it?
column2: Step 8: a line-by-line spreadsheet with scene numbers and a unique file name/ID per line.

column1: Name three books Rogers recommends for deeper screenwriting study.
column2: Syd Field's Screenplay, Robert McKee's Story, Lew Hunter's Screenwriting 434.

column1: Why bring character images to a voice session?
column2: They help actors (who often play several parts) bring each character to life; send them early to aid casting.

column1: Why encourage actor improvisation?
column2: More material and alternate takes, actors enjoy it, and they'll want to work with you again.

column1: Your team wants a 10,000-troop siege as an in-engine (puppet show) beat on the meta screen. Which step warns you?
column2: Step 2: break scenes down by characters and locations for staging and asset creation; puppet shows can't show huge armies.

column1: In your event beat, the player taps a lever and a door opens off-screen; players are confused. Fix?
column2: Show clear cause and effect: start the camera from the player's position and pan to the door as it opens.

column1: When was FMV popular, and which game systems were built around it?
column2: It boomed when games first moved to CD media, and in the mid-1990s systems like the 3DO, Philips CD-i and Sega Mega CD specialized in FMV-heavy interactive movies.

column1: What does Rogers' Tekken 3 anecdote warn about prerendered cutscenes?
column2: Spectacular cinematics were made by just two animators who both ended up hospitalized from exhaustion: cinematic quality costs money, time and manpower, so don't pay for it with crunch.

column1: Complete: Rogers played 'Name That Tune' with dialogue by bidding '12 lines' versus '____ lines or less'.
column2: Eight. The point is to keep trimming the dialogue.

column1: Rogers says there are many ways to make cutscenes, just like movies. Name all six.
column2: The six are FMV, animated, Flash-animated, prerendered, puppet show and scripted event.

column1: What is a pitch, according to Level 17?
column2: A streamlined, easily digestible version of your GDD containing everything great and original about the game.

column1: What are "twiddley bits"?
column2: Industry slang for hard-won details that matter for making the game but not for selling it; leave them out of the pitch.

column1: What must you find before you can make the game, and what do you need to find it?
column2: A publisher, and to find one you need a pitch.

column1: What software does Rogers recommend for pitches, and why?
column2: Presentation software like PowerPoint, because most pitches are presented to groups in boardrooms.

column1: List the five basics of a pitch presentation.
column2: Opening slide with logo; company profile; high concept; a handful of detail pages; proof it will be awesome and profitable.

column1: Which Bonus Level holds the full pitch presentation outline?
column2: Bonus Level 9.

column1: Name the three slide-design basics Rogers reminds you of.
column2: Readable font; don't put too much info on one slide; everyone loves pictures.

column1: Pitching is like putting together an artist's ____.
column2: portfolio (best work only, not so many pieces that you overwhelm)

column1: Why did Rogers tune out the Nebulon/Galactic Imperium story pitch?
column2: Too much lore to process at once; he only wanted to know how the game played.

column1: What should you do with your world's story details at pitch stage?
column2: Keep it simple and keep them to yourself for now.

column1: Name the six rules of thumb for pitching.
column2: Pitch to the right people; controlled environment; be prepared; know your project inside and out; keep the focus; pitch to represent.

column1: Why research a publisher before pitching?
column2: Some publishers only publish certain genres; otherwise you hear "great pitch, but we'd never publish that" and waste everyone's time.

column1: Controlled environment: pitching on the E3 show floor = bad; pitching in a private ____ at E3 = much better.
column2: meeting room

column1: If a teammate is a better speaker, what does Rogers advise?
column2: Let them present under your supervision, and still attend to answer questions and fill in details.

column1: What is Rogers' ultimate preparedness test for a pitch?
column2: Could you still make your pitch if the power went out?

column1: Name four items from the book's pitch-kit illustration.
column2: Any four: eye contact, enthusiasm/smile, dress accordingly, business cards, take-away documentation, playable demo, laptop, flash/backup drive, projectable PowerPoint or video.

column1: Why do publishers ask hole-poking questions in pitches?
column2: Not malice: they're looking for issues that could cause trouble once production starts.

column1: What can you say when you don't know the answer to a publisher's question?
column2: Invite their thoughts on it (turn it into a conversation).

column1: Name the three problems with bringing several pitches to one meeting.
column2: Longer meeting; less time per game; possibly no consensus on the best idea.

column1: If you present several ideas anyway, what's the rule?
column2: All presentations must be at the same level of quality.

column1: Why might you pitch with only great tech or a prototype mechanic?
column2: A publisher may hold a license with no studio chosen; timing and luck matter as much as the idea.

column1: Write Rogers' pitch equation.
column2: Game demo > game design document > presentation > pitch.

column1: GAME DEMO > ____ > PRESENTATION > PITCH
column2: GAME DESIGN DOCUMENT

column1: Why are demos risky for production?
column2: They're a lot of work, take time from the main game, disrupt flow and can cause crunch.

column1: Why are demos still worth it?
column2: They show you're serious and let publishers get hands on code, sometimes the best way to sell a game.

column1: Rogers' bolded very important thing: video games are made by ____.
column2: people

column1: According to Rogers, what causes most games that go badly?
column2: Bad planning.

column1: Name two publisher-side reasons a good game can sell poorly.
column2: Publisher can't fund enough promotion; sales projections set at unreachable levels.

column1: What should "plan ahead" cover, per the troubleshooting list?
column2: Team illnesses and vacations; hardware failure, brown-outs and other technical issues.

column1: Why lock down design and content as early as possible?
column2: Constant changes chasing perfection wear the team down and can kill the game.

column1: How should you playtest to find breakage?
column2: Play like players: do unusual things, bang on it until it breaks, then fix it.

column1: What did Fat Princess change for its Japanese release?
column2: Its four-fingered characters were redesigned with five fingers.

column1: Give the three explanations for the four-finger taboo in Japan.
column2: Yubitsume (Yakuza finger-cutting); four (shi) also means death; a four-finger sign was a slur against the Burakumin.

column1: What are design blinders?
column2: Being too close to your game, so you think it's too easy or half-baked elements are "good enough."

column1: What is the "10,000 foot view"?
column2: An objective outside look at your game (publishers excel at it) that spots weak spots and strengthens good parts.

column1: S.I.F.S. stands for: save it for the ____.
column2: sequel

column1: Why shouldn't throwing out work become a habit?
column2: Planning ahead to anticipate problems is better than wasting work.

column1: The more you cut in ____, the less you'll cut in production.
column2: preproduction

column1: What kind of content should you NOT cut or change?
column2: Content connected to and affecting multiple game systems.

column1: Define a vertical slice.
column2: A level or sequence designed, built and polished to the highest playability and quality of every discipline; a publisher demo and template for the game.

column1: A vertical slice usually targets about ____% of final game quality.
Define a horizontal layer.
column2: Bringing all elements of the game, beginning to end, up at once in gray box, then polishing after playtesting and approval.

column1: What's usually missing in a gray box level?
column2: Texturing, effects and sound; geometry is rough and animation mostly placeholder.

column1: Why keep concept art on hand when showing gray box?
column2: Viewers must use their imagination, which is rare, so concept art stops them getting the wrong idea.

column1: What's the book's example of a gray-box discovery?
column2: Bouncing off enemies' heads turns out more fun than fighting them, so the design adjusts.

column1: Rogers' complaint: designers use emergent gameplay as an excuse to underdesign, hoping the player will "____."
column2: find the fun

column1: Define emergent gameplay.
column2: Gameplay that "just happens" when players get a set of tools and a chance to play with them.

column1: What's Rogers' problem with emergent gameplay?
column2: Designers use it as an excuse to underdesign, hoping players will "find the fun."

column1: What does Rogers call the secret to successful game production?
column2: Planning ahead.

column1: Why do publishers like sequels?
column2: They're safe(r) bets: proven IP that doesn't need explaining, like Hollywood sequels.

column1: What limits does a team face on a first game that a sequel removes?
column2: Building a team and engine, figuring out the character and gameplay, making it work and be fun, hoping people buy it.

column1: What happened with Rogers' Maximo sequel fix list?
column2: He listed 40 broken things and got 39 fixed; the first sold better, but the sequel was the better game.

column1: What is George Collins' 30/70 rule?
column2: A sequel should be 30% new material and ideas, 70% based on the original game.

column1: What sequel naming does Rogers recommend?
column2: Not "GameName 2": titles like Batman Returns or "Indiana Jones and the..." that are mysterious and extend the fiction.

column1: What new content should every sequel have?
column2: Five new back-of-box features (preferably gameplay) and at least one new hero and villain.

column1: What went wrong in Maximo vs. Army of Zin?
column2: Players wanted supernatural enemies but got clockwork creatures; fans were unhappy.

column1: Which franchises does Rogers cite as successful late reinventions?
column2: Grand Theft Auto and Wolfenstein.

column1: What are the four closing rules of the book?
column2: Take breaks; be fair and generous; keep playing games, even bad ones; enjoy it (you could be flipping burgers).

column1: Why be fair and generous in games, per Rogers?
column2: It's a very small industry and word gets around fast.

column1: In the chili analogy, what does the boil represent, and its danger?
column2: Crunch time; boil too long and you burn the pot, i.e., too much crunch can destroy games and studios.

column1: In the chili analogy, what is the recipe and what is the simmer?
column2: Recipe = documentation; simmer = polish, iteration and bug fixing.

column1: Why should a sequel be a better game than the original?
column2: The hard part is done: team, engine, character and gameplay are figured out, so you can focus on fixing and perfecting.

column1: Why is a vertical slice also called a template?
column2: It sets the quality bar and approach the rest of the game should match.

column1: Your lead designer mumbles in meetings; your producer is a natural showman. Who should give the pitch?
column2: The producer, under the designer's supervision, with the designer present to answer questions (be prepared).

column1: Your studio has no original concept but has built impressive mobile physics tech. Should you pitch?
column2: Yes: pitch to represent; a publisher may have a license and need a studio with your tech.

column1: Your F2P pitch deck spends six slides on your world's history before showing gameplay. Which section title warns you?
column2: No One Cares About Your Stupid Little World: keep lore to yourself and show how it plays.

column1: After launch, players skip timers by changing their device clock. Which troubleshooting item should have caught it?
column2: Play the game like players and bang on it until it breaks (in F2P: QA the economy).

column1: Six months before soft launch, your team is still reworking level 1 every week chasing perfection. Which rule applies?
column2: Lock down design and content as early as possible; constant changes wear the team down and can kill the game.

column1: A season update removes the mode your most loyal players love. Which sequel rule is broken?
column2: Don't let the player down: keep what fans loved (the wall-running rule).

column1: Your F2P team wants to bring three concepts to one publisher meeting "to see what sticks." Which Rogers rule applies?
column2: Keep the focus: one standout idea; extra pitches lengthen the meeting, dilute attention and block consensus.

column1: A designer insists on keeping a clunky camera in the sequel "because it was in the first game." Which principle?
column2: Use the spine of the original: keep the good, cut the bad; legacy isn't a justification.

column1: Playtesters say your FTUE is confusing, but your team thinks it's obvious. Which concept explains the gap?
column2: Design blinders; fix with outside playtests and the "10,000 foot view" (in F2P, funnels and A/B tests).

column1: Your economy designer says "players will find the fun in how the currencies interact." Which Rogers warning?
column2: Emergent, eschmergent: don't rely on emergence; plan and model the interactions (sources and sinks).

column1: You're launching a gacha game in Japan, China and Belgium. Which troubleshooting item applies?
column2: Account for cultural (and regulatory) differences in international versions, like Fat Princess's five fingers.

column1: Late in production you want to cut a currency sink that feeds three systems. What does Rogers warn?
column2: Don't cut content connected to multiple systems; cut early, in preproduction, for the right reasons.

column1: Your LiveOps plan needs a new event every week from a 3-person team with no buffer. Which truth is being violated?
column2: Video games are made by people: schedule for people issues and avoid crunch with responsible goals and planning.

column1: Your F2P successor game changes the art style, genre and characters all at once. Which sequel rule warns you?
column2: Don't make it too new (Army of Zin); follow 30/70 and keep what fans loved.

column1: A publisher asks for proof your F2P concept will retain players. Per the pitch equation, what's strongest to bring?
column2: A playable build with real test metrics (demo beats doc beats slides beats talk).

column1: How many people does the book's chili recipe feed, and what are its two timings?
column2: Feeds 6 to 8; brown the brisket about 7–10 minutes, then simmer covered about 2–2½ hours.

column1: Give the nine steps of the chili method in short form.
column2: 1 Brown garlic, then brisket. 2 Purée anchos with broth. 3 Meat to a plate, pour off oil, add purée and tomatoes. 4 Stir in dry spices. 5 Boil, then simmer covered. 6 Chunk peppers and onion. 7 Shred meat with forks, return with veg, adjust seasoning. 8 Boil off most of the liquid. 9 Serve topped with cheese, sour cream, scallions.

column1: Which chili spices get a full tablespoon, and what are the topping amounts?
column2: Cayenne and garlic salt (Lowry's) get 1 tbsp each; chili powder and crushed red chili get ½ tbsp. Toppings: ¼ cup scallions, ½ cup sour cream, ½ cup shredded Monterey Jack. The oil is ¼ cup.

column1: What three questions does the book's Slide 9 (Production Specs) in the pitch outline answer?
column2: How big the dedicated team is, how long the game will take to make, and how much it will cost.

column1: An investor asks "how many people, how long, how much?" Which pitch slide answers that, and what do you add for F2P?
column2: Production Specs (Bonus Level 9, Slide 9); in F2P add milestone dates for prototype, soft launch and global launch.

column1: What are the two jobs of a one-sheet?
column2: Keep the team and managers aligned on priorities and objectives, and excite outside readers about the game.

column1: Which outside readers is a one-sheet meant to be handed to?
column2: Management, marketing, sales and licensors.

column1: On a one-sheet, the ____ matters more than the style.
column2: information

column1: Which two one-sheet formats does Bonus Level 1 show?
column2: A text-only version and a version with images.

column1: What's the "victory" sign that your one-sheet has sunk in?
column2: A teammate pushes back on a feature because it contradicts the one-sheet, and they're right.

column1: Maximum number of USPs on a one-sheet?
Which three qualities make a good comp?
column2: Successful, recent, very well known (ideally all three).

column1: Which comps does the Farm Wars one-sheet cite?
column2: Tower-defense games, the Harvest Moon series and Lock's Quest.

column1: Why should a one-sheet summary include beginning/middle/end, play style and objectives?
column2: So one short paragraph shows the hook, what the player does and why, enough to judge the concept.

column1: How detailed should the one-sheet's game outline be?
column2: Deeper than the summary, but not in great detail.

column1: Your one-pager lists 11 USPs. What's the fix?
column2: Cut to the 5–7 strongest that show play style, modes, multiplayer, tech or cool features.

column1: Why does the Maximo one-sheet put a gameplay-promise headline above each location?
column2: So each place sells a verb or feature, making the strip a level list, feature list and story outline at once.

column1: Why are Maximo's "telling traits" (sword, underwear, Death sidekick) valuable on a one-sheet?
column2: They're specific, visual and marketable hooks, far more memorable than generic adjectives.

column1: The ten-pager is a set of ____ rather than strict policy.
column2: guidelines

column1: What does the ten-pager's foundation later turn into?
column2: The pitch and the GDD.

column1: What goes on ten-pager page 1 (title page)?
column2: Graphic, title (ideally a logo), contact info, target platform, audience, rating, expected ship date.

column1: What does ten-pager page 3, Game flow, answer?
column2: How the player grows as challenges increase, how it ties to story, the growth systems (XP, money, score, collectibles) and what's gained.

column1: Which hardware features does the ten-pager's page 5 use as examples?
column2: Hard drive, touch screen, multiple screens, memory card.

column1: Your ten-pager describes screens but never says how players move between menus or what music plays there. Which page is missing?
column2: The Interface page: shell navigation, mood of the screens, music, and an interface flow diagram.

column1: What does ten-pager page 10 cover?
column2: Cutscenes (presentation, timing, format), unlockables and replay incentive, and the competition at release.

column1: The five phases of a Farm Wars round (ten-pager)?
column2: Buying, planting, defending, boss, selling.

column1: Farm Wars win and lose conditions?
column2: Win: survive and defeat all animal bosses. Lose: go broke, farm devastated, or get killed.

column1: Which three references make up Farm Wars' elevator pitch?
column2: FarmVille, tower defense, MechWarrior (an X meets Y meets Z formula).

column1: Farm Wars' sample defensive tech progression?
column2: Fence < barbed wire < electric fence < force field < laser system.

column1: Why do Farm Wars enemies attack crops and structures, not just the player?
column2: It ties combat to the farming/economy loop, so every enemy matters to both.

column1: Why do details differ between the Farm Wars one-sheet, ten-pager and pitch?
column2: Designs evolve; documents are living, which is why version numbers and revision history matter.

column1: Why does the Farm Wars ten-pager plan cutscenes as puppet-show sequences built from in-game assets?
column2: Reusing in-game assets keeps cutscenes short, cheap to make and consistent with the game's look.

column1: Which genres is the GDD template skewed toward?
column2: Action, adventure, platform, RPG and shooter (adaptable to any style).

column1: In a GDD, a "____" is better than nothing at all.
column2: TBD

column1: What two forces make GDD content change, per Bonus Level 3?
column2: Technology limitations and production-time realities.

column1: What goes on the GDD cover?
column2: Cover image, title, document version, written by (team), point of contact with phone, publishing date, version number.

column1: What must every GDD footer show?
column2: Copyright/company/date, page number, current date.

column1: What does the GDD's Game goals section include?
column2: The high concept, back-of-box new/novel features, and all Internet and wireless features.

column1: Three parts of the GDD story overview?
column2: Set-up, locations and how the player gets between them, finale.

column1: Your GDD's tech section has grown to 30 pages of engine detail. What does Bonus Level 3 advise?
column2: Keep it brief in the GDD and move the detail into the technical design document (TDD).

column1: Which cheat tools does the GDD template propose?
column2: Level, invulnerability, camera, and others like full health/armor/money.

column1: Which boot credit screens does the GDD front end list?
column2: Publisher, studio logo, licensors, third-party software makers, legal screen.

column1: What is attract mode?
column2: In-game material that plays if the game is left idle on the start screen.

column1: Which camera types does the GDD template list?
column2: First person, third person, three-quarters, 2.5-D, forced scroll, spline, locked.

column1: Name six HUD elements from the GDD template.
column2: Any six: health/status, lives/continues, money/score/rank, power/fuel, ammo, abilities, timer, map, option links, plings, reticule, speedometer.

column1: Your game has no HUD. What does the GDD template still require?
column2: A description of how health, ammo, map and similar info will be conveyed to the player.

column1: The four melee combat reactions in the GDD?
column2: Block, dodge, parry, grab.

column1: Why does the GDD ask for the yield percentage of breakable objects?
column2: Drop rates shape the reward flow, so designers and programmers need exact, tunable numbers.

column1: What do the GDD's general enemy rules cover?
column2: Behavior types (patroller, hunter, flyer), how the AI senses the player (detection numbers), where and when enemies spawn, what counts as defeating them, and the rules for loot payouts.

column1: Your music list covers every level. Which tracks does the GDD template remind you might still be missing?
column2: Title, pause, options and end-credits music.

column1: You're writing a GDD for a mobile match-3. Which major sections must you add to the 2010 template?
column2: Economy, monetization, FTUE, retention/LiveOps, analytics/KPIs (and compliance).

column1: How is the story-themes list organized?
column2: Alphabetically, with "Family: flavor" sub-genres (Adventure, Comedy, Fantasy, Horror, Sci-fi, Sports, War) plus standalone genres.

column1: Which theme family is biggest in Bonus Level 4?
column2: Sci-fi, with seven flavors.

column1: Which scale modifiers appear in the environments list?
column2: Giant-sized world, a shrunken "little" world, inside/on top of a giant creature.

column1: The event team needs a cheap new event. How can Bonus Level 5 help?
column2: Re-skin a known mode in a new environment (plus music and a themed currency), or apply a scale flip.

column1: Name the main families of Bonus Level 6 objects.
column2: Movers/traversal, timing hazards, area hazards, gates, interactive puzzle props, and rewards like chests and dispensers.

column1: A match-3 blocker needs two matches to clear. Which Bonus Level 6 item is its ancestor?
column2: The two-stage openable/breakable object.

column1: What's in the enemy template's animation list?
column2: Stand, idle, taunts, melee attacks, projectile attacks, hit reactions, death animations, victory animations.

column1: Why match the SFX and voice lists to the animation list?
column2: Every animation gets its sounds, and any gap reveals a forgotten asset.

column1: An enemy's attack freezes the hero in ice. Which enemy-template field captures the extra work this creates?
column2: Special requirements for player character (the hero needs a frozen animation/VFX).

column1: What does the boss template add to the enemy template's fields?
column2: Weak spots/vulnerable states, the health bar's look, a guaranteed reward, and the arena page.

column1: The four Boss Fight Arena fields?
column2: Arena image, arena description, level elements, boss fight music tracks (incl. contextual music).

column1: The nine high-concept pitch slides, in order?
column2: Cover, company profile, target specs, game story, game goals, gameplay summary, gameplay details, download strategy, production specs.

column1: Why put the presentation date on the pitch cover?
column2: So the people you present to remember when the meeting took place.

column1: Why credit the studio rather than yourself on the pitch?
column2: No one makes a game by themselves.

column1: You're pitching to your own studio's leadership. Which slide can you skip?
column2: The company profile slide.

column1: What four questions does the target specs slide answer?
column2: What kind of game, its rating, its audience, how long it takes to play.

column1: Aim for ____ "back of the box" goals on the pitch.
column2: five

column1: What three things does the production specs slide answer?
column2: Team size, development time, cost.

column1: Your F2P pitch has no slide on events or seasons. What's missing?
column2: The modern download strategy: a retention and LiveOps plan.

column1: An exec asks how you'll acquire players. Which F2P pitch slides answer it?
column2: The UA & marketing hook (ad creatives, CPI target, ASO) plus target KPIs (LTV vs. CPI).

column1: Why does the boss template insist on weak spots or vulnerable states?
column2: They define the boss puzzle: how the player learns and exploits openings.

column1: Why does a GDD need a game flowchart?
column2: It shows how every screen from title to game over connects, so nothing is a dead end.

column1: Your ten-pager is 14 pages but covers every topic clearly and is fun to read. Problem?
column2: Not really: ten pages is a guideline; coverage and readability matter. Trim only if it bores readers.

column1: Teammates keep proposing features that drift off-vision. Which Bonus Level 1 habit helps?
column2: Reiterate the one-sheet's points every time you discuss the game.

column1: Why put concrete numbers (6 maps, 15–30 min rounds, 10+ hours) into a ten-pager?
column2: They make scope believable and let producers estimate.

column1: You're designing an F2P event boss with a continue offer. What's the guardrail?
column2: It must be beatable without paying; continues via soft currency or rewarded ad, never cash-only.

column1: Why do mobile docs replace controller maps with gesture maps?
column2: There are no buttons; touch gestures, thumb reach and haptics define control.

column1: You need a fresh level concept in one minute. How do Bonus Levels 4–6 help?
column2: Combine a story theme + an environment + a mechanic (optionally flip the scale).

column1: Boss arena music notes should include ____ music.
column2: contextual

column1: Farm Wars' defensive tech progression ends with the ____ system.
column2: laser

column1: Which ten-pager page did the Farm Wars sample leave out entirely?
column2: The Interface page (comps lived on the one-sheet instead).

column1: Name four families of environment on the Big List beyond natural biomes and city streets.
column2: Any four of: military and conflict zones, faith/death/spooky places, water and coast, commerce/food/nightlife, rural and green spaces, transport hubs, cultural districts and landmarks.

column1: Which items on the Mechanics and Hazards list are tools the player operates rather than hazards that act on the player?
column2: Levers, cranks/pumps, pressure plates, push blocks, shootable targets and carryable/throwable objects (plus keys and doors they unlock).

column1: Roughly how many entries do the three Bonus Level idea lists hold: themes, environments, mechanics/hazards?
column2: About 48 story themes, about 150 environments and about 35 mechanics and hazards.

column1: Your world list is forest, jungle, swamp, then another forest. What does the environments-list advice suggest?
column2: Audit it by family and mood: vary colour, mood and hazards, and use scale or theme flips (giant world, shrunken player) to break up the greens.

column1: What does F2P mean, and where does its money come from?
column2: Free-to-play: free to download and play; revenue comes from optional in-app purchases and/or ads.

column1: What is a consumable IAP?
column2: A purchase that gets used up: gems, boosters, extra moves, energy refills.

column1: What is a durable (non-consumable) IAP?
column2: A purchase you keep forever: a hero, a skin, "remove ads", a permanent extra builder.

column1: What is a rewarded video ad?
column2: An opt-in ad the player chooses to watch in exchange for a reward (revive, double coins, free chest).

column1: What is an interstitial ad?
column2: A full-screen ad shown between levels or sessions that the player didn't opt into.

column1: What does AARRR ("pirate metrics") stand for?
column2: Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, Revenue.

column1: What is a soft launch?
column2: A quiet release in a few test countries to measure retention and monetization before global launch.

column1: How is stickiness calculated?
column2: DAU ÷ MAU.

column1: What is a cohort?
column2: A group of players analysed together, usually everyone who installed on the same day.

column1: What does D7 retention measure?
column2: The % of an install cohort who play on day 7 after installing.

column1: Classic vs rolling retention?
column2: Classic: active exactly on day N. Rolling: active on day N or any later day (always higher).

column1: What is ARPDAU?
column2: Average revenue per daily active user = daily revenue ÷ DAU.

column1: What is ARPPU?
column2: Average revenue per paying user = revenue ÷ number of payers.

column1: What is (payer) conversion?
column2: The % of players who make at least one purchase.

column1: What is eCPM?
column2: Effective ad revenue per 1,000 ad impressions.

column1: What is ROAS?
column2: Return on ad spend: a cohort's revenue ÷ the UA money spent to acquire it.

column1: What is the payback period?
column2: The number of days until a cohort's revenue covers its acquisition cost (ROAS = 100%).

column1: What is the K-factor?
column2: How many new players each player brings in; above 1 means self-sustaining viral growth.

column1: What is a churn point?
column2: A specific place where many players quit, such as a tutorial step or a particular level.

column1: What is Goodhart's law?
column2: When a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure.

column1: What are the four steps of a core loop diagram?
column2: Action → Reward → Invest → New power / new challenge → back to Action.

column1: Name the three loop layers and their timescales.
column2: Core (seconds–minutes), mid/daily (a session to a day), meta (days–months); LiveOps sits on top.

column1: What are the four steps of Nir Eyal's Hook model?
column2: Trigger → action → variable reward → investment.

column1: What are the four parts of the session arc?
column2: Arrive & collect → core play → invest & set up → exit hook.

column1: What is the Zeigarnik effect?
column2: People remember unfinished tasks better than finished ones, so open loops pull players back.

column1: What does FTUE stand for?
column2: First-Time User Experience.

column1: What is progressive disclosure?
column2: Hiding UI and features until they unlock, so early screens stay simple.

column1: Vertical vs horizontal progression?
column2: Vertical = more power (stats). Horizontal = more options (new heroes, cards, strategies).

column1: What is power creep?
column2: New content that is stronger than old content, making earlier items obsolete.

column1: What is the goal-gradient effect?
column2: Motivation increases as a goal gets closer.

column1: What is the flow channel?
column2: The zone where challenge matches skill: too hard causes anxiety, too easy causes boredom (Csikszentmihalyi).

column1: What is saw-tooth difficulty?
column2: Difficulty ramps to a spike, drops to a breather, then climbs again, with an overall upward trend.

column1: What are faucets and drains?
column2: Faucets (sources) add currency to the economy; drains (sinks) remove it.

column1: Name the six sink families.
column2: Progression, consumable, convenience/time, chance, cosmetic/luxury, social.

column1: What is a starter pack?
column2: A one-time, very high-value, low-price offer shown early to turn non-payers into payers.

column1: What is a pity system?
column2: A guarantee of a top-rarity reward after a set number of pulls without one.

column1: Name five energy-system parameters.
column2: Cap, regen rate, cost per attempt, overflow rules, refill price.

column1: Name Bartle's four player types.
column2: Achievers, Explorers, Socializers, Killers.

column1: Name Quantic Foundry's six motivation groups.
column2: Action, Social, Mastery, Achievement, Immersion, Creativity.

column1: What does MDA stand for?
column2: Mechanics, Dynamics, Aesthetics (Hunicke, LeBlanc & Zubek).

column1: What is confirmshaming?
column2: Wording a decline button to shame the player, e.g. "No thanks, I like losing".

column1: What does DDA mean?
column2: Dynamic difficulty adjustment: quietly tuning difficulty to the player, e.g. easing a level after repeated fails.

column1: How do you calculate playtime per day?
column2: Session length × sessions per day.

column1: Why are non-paying players valuable?
column2: They are opponents/clanmates (liquidity), spread the game, watch ads, and may pay later.

column1: Why fix retention before monetization?
column2: LTV multiplies retention × engagement × monetization: players who left can't pay.

column1: Why should KPIs be read by cohort?
column2: Blended averages mix countries, platforms and traffic sources and hide real changes.

column1: Why do many designers avoid the term "compulsion loop"?
column2: It implies manipulating players; "core loop" is the neutral term.

column1: Why must a core loop change as it repeats?
column2: If the investment doesn't make the next round feel different, the loop becomes a grind.

column1: Why build the FTUE last and then rebuild it often?
column2: You only know what to teach at the end, and every player passes through it, so it's the highest-leverage feature.

column1: Why ask for notification permission after showing value?
column2: Players accept when they understand the benefit, and an early "no" is hard to undo.

column1: Why does saw-tooth difficulty work?
column2: Spikes test mastery, breathers give relief and a feeling of power, and the rhythm adds variety.

column1: Why can exponential XP curves create accidental walls?
column2: They look gentle early, then explode late, overtaking polynomial curves.

column1: Why use separate soft and hard currencies?
